    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.4

    Visibility, cancellation & overload

    Prerequisites: 4.3 · Shared memory & coordination4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Build a service that processes 1,000 file uploads. Compare sequential execution, threads, asynchronous I/O, and worker queues. Identify which architecture helps under which workload.

    This chapter examines visibility, cancellation & overload through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    4.4.1 · Memory visibility and happens-before relationships

    Visibility is not established by intuition about elapsed time. A writer's update and another thread's read need the ordering guarantees defined by the language and synchronization primitives. Happens-before is a formal relation used to reason about such guarantees, not a statement that every earlier wall-clock event is visible. Publish an immutable object through a synchronized channel or appropriate atomic reference. The Go memory model is one concrete specification; other languages must be checked separately.

    4.4.2 · Thread safety and immutability

    Thread safety is a behavioral property under a stated concurrent-use contract. Immutable values avoid mutation races after safe publication, but references, initialization, and surrounding resources still need ownership rules. A frozen task record can be shared; a mutable cache mapping task IDs to records may still need synchronization. Avoid returning writable internal collections. Confinement, immutability, locks, and message ownership are complementary tools, with copying and coordination costs that depend on the workload.

    4.4.3 · Resource exhaustion and backpressure

    Unlimited concurrency converts downstream slowness into memory and connection exhaustion. Backpressure bounds or slows producers according to available capacity. For an assumed worker rate of 100 jobs/s and arrivals of 150 jobs/s, a queue grows by fifty jobs/s until a limit is reached. A larger queue delays rejection but does not fix the rate mismatch. Prefer bounded queues, admission deadlines, compact payloads, and explicit overload responses; monitor queue age as well as length.

    4.4.4 · Cancellation and structured concurrency

    Cancellation must propagate to owned child work and release resources. Structured concurrency ties child-task lifetimes to a parent scope, so failures and completion have an explicit owner. Cancelling a caller does not prove an external side effect was undone: a payment may already have committed. Use finally-style cleanup for local resources and reconciliation for uncertain remote effects. Detached tasks need a durable owner when their business outcome must survive the request process.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Pseudocode · bounded upload ownership

    queue = bounded_queue(capacity=100)
start_workers(count=50)
for upload in arrivals:
    reference = persist_upload_or_reject(upload)
    queue.put_with_deadline(reference)
worker():
    while reference = queue.take():
        try: process(reference)
        finally: release_owned_resources()

    The queue bounds waiting references and the worker count bounds active execution. Large bytes remain in storage. The durable job and rejection policy must account for a queue handoff failure; a process-local queue alone is not durable work acceptance.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · CALCULATED TEACHING MODEL

    A bigger queue cannot repair a permanent rate mismatch

    Fluid approximation with constant rates and initially empty waiting queue. The model accounts for completed, waiting, and rejected work; real scheduling, startup, and per-job variance are omitted.

    1,000 uploads · compare the resource that dominates

    Assume each independent upload needs exactly 100 ms of waiting for storage and no meaningful CPU work. Ignore startup, connection limits, bandwidth, queue overhead, and variance. Sequential execution then needs 100 seconds; allowing 50 independent waits at once has an ideal lower bound of 2 seconds. These are constructed lower bounds, not measurements.

    Same I/O workload, different execution and recovery boundaries
    Execution modelIdeal elapsed timeWhat must be boundedCrash recovery
    Sequential100 sOne active upload; backlog elsewhereRequires a durable record
    50 threads with blocking I/O2 sThreads, stacks, connectionsMemory alone loses accepted work
    Async I/O with 50 in flight2 sTasks, buffers, socketsMemory alone loses accepted work
    Durable queue, 50 workersAt least 2 s, plus queue overheadAdmission, queue age, worker countDurable intent plus retry and idempotent completion

    Change the workload: each upload instead requires 20 ms of CPU and negligible I/O. The batch needs 20 CPU-seconds. One executing core therefore needs at least 20 seconds; eight truly parallel cores have an ideal lower bound of 2.5 seconds. An event loop creates no extra cores. Runtime restrictions can also prevent CPU-heavy threads from running in parallel. Measure overhead and contention before choosing threads or processes. A durable queue changes acknowledgment and recovery behavior; it does not erase service demand.

    Show A-read-zero, B-read-zero, A-write-one, B-write-one before repairing the critical section. Bound queued payload references and active workers separately. For I/O waiting, compare concurrency; for CPU work, account for runtime parallelism. An async keyword alone does not repair the race or add CPU capacity.

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.1

    Model behavior with objects and values

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Start with a poorly designed payment-processing class. Refactor it into appropriate components, showing which problems each design improvement solves.

    This chapter examines model behavior with objects and values through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    5.1.1 · Abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance

    A payment class that validates an order, creates a provider SDK, calculates fees, and writes audit records hides several reasons to change. Abstraction exposes charge(command); encapsulation protects payment state; polymorphism permits different implementations of a behavior. Inheritance is one mechanism for sharing and specializing behavior, not a requirement for these benefits. Extract provider communication behind a contract while keeping the amount and allowed state transitions under application control.

    5.1.2 · Composition vs inheritance

    A subclass can violate assumptions inherited by callers: a ReadOnlyAccount subclass that throws from withdraw is not substitutable for a contract promising withdrawal. Composition combines collaborators through explicit contracts instead. A payment service receiving a fraud policy and a gateway can vary them independently without a subclass for every combination. Composition introduces wiring and interface design; inheritance remains useful when the behavioral relationship is genuinely stable, rather than merely when two classes share fields.

    5.1.3 · Interfaces and contracts

    A gateway interface must specify currency, amount units, timeouts, duplicate identity, and error meaning. charge(100) is ambiguous: one currency unit, one hundred, or one hundred minor units? Return a structured outcome such as approved, declined, or uncertain with a provider reference. A transport exception after submission is not proof of decline. Behavioral contracts let adapters be replaced without silently changing business semantics, but require integration tests against real provider behavior.

    5.1.4 · High cohesion and low coupling

    Cohesion improves when related payment rules live together; coupling falls when business code does not depend on provider-specific field names. Measure the effect using a change: adding an SMS receipt should not alter ledger arithmetic. Several focused modules may still share one deployment. Excessive fragmentation can make a simple path harder to follow, so extract a responsibility when it owns an invariant, hides unstable knowledge, or supports a concrete change independently.

    5.1.5 · SOLID principles, including their limitations

    SOLID is a set of design heuristics: single responsibility, open/closed extension, behavioral substitution, focused interfaces, and dependency inversion. A payment service can depend on a narrow charge contract while its adapter depends on an SDK. These ideas do not require one interface per class or forbid editing existing code. An extension mechanism with twenty configuration switches may be harder to understand than a deliberate edit. Judge each heuristic against the actual change and testing cost.

    Architecture review · Which payment abstractions remain useful if the implementation moves from objects to pure functions?

    Test approved, declined, and uncertain outcomes without real charges. Keep integer units and currency explicit. A test fake validates orchestration only; real serialization, timeouts, and persistence need separate integration evidence. Do not map a timeout to decline simply to make a test pass.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    An extension mechanism with twenty configuration switches may be harder to understand than a deliberate edit.

    Carry forward: Separate reasons to change · Preserve behavioral substitution · Keep collaborator contracts narrow · Invert unstable dependency knowledge.

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.2

    Principles under pressure

    Prerequisites: 5.1 · Model behavior with objects and values4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Start with a poorly designed payment-processing class. Refactor it into appropriate components, showing which problems each design improvement solves.

    This chapter examines principles under pressure through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    5.2.1 · DRY, KISS, YAGNI

    DRY avoids duplicated knowledge, not every repeated line. KISS prefers a design understandable for the required behavior; YAGNI defers speculative capability. Two similar validations may represent different policies and should not be merged solely for visual similarity. Conversely, copying the same currency conversion rule into every gateway creates a real consistency risk. Share a stable business concept after identifying its owner, and keep a reversible simple implementation until evidence justifies a larger abstraction.

    5.2.2 · Law of Demeter

    The Law of Demeter discourages reaching deeply through another object's internal graph. order.customer.account.settings.currency exposes representation and creates change propagation. Ask an appropriate owner for the information or behavior needed, such as order.paymentCurrency(). It is a heuristic, not a ban on every fluent API or data traversal. Adding dozens of meaningless forwarding methods can obscure the model; the objective is to reduce knowledge of unstable structure, not count dots in source code.

    5.2.3 · Tell, Don't Ask

    Tell, Don't Ask encourages sending an intention to the state owner. Rather than reading account.balance, comparing it outside, and writing it back, request reserve(amount) so the account can enforce its invariant. Reading a value for a report remains appropriate. The principle does not authorize hiding surprising side effects behind getters. The owner must still coordinate concurrent changes at the true shared-state boundary, such as an atomic database transaction.

    5.2.4 · Command-query separation

    Command-query separation distinguishes operations that change state from queries that report it. A payment status getter should not unexpectedly charge a card. Some practical commands return useful results, such as the created payment identifier, without violating the underlying intent of clear side effects. Document these conventions. Separating read and write models into CQRS is a larger architectural choice; ordinary command-query separation does not require separate services, databases, or event sourcing.

    Architecture review · Which payment abstractions remain useful if the implementation moves from objects to pure functions?

    Test approved, declined, and uncertain outcomes without real charges. Keep integer units and currency explicit. A test fake validates orchestration only; real serialization, timeouts, and persistence need separate integration evidence. Do not map a timeout to decline simply to make a test pass.

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.3

    Side effects, domain models & collaboration

    Prerequisites: 5.2 · Principles under pressure4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Start with a poorly designed payment-processing class. Refactor it into appropriate components, showing which problems each design improvement solves.

    This chapter examines side effects, domain models & collaboration through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    5.3.1 · Immutability and side-effect management

    Immutable values make state transitions easier to inspect: compute a new PaymentSummary from an old value rather than mutating a shared object in several helpers. Keep effectful operations at explicit boundaries and pass their results into pure calculations. Immutability can cost allocation and copying, and cannot undo a provider charge. An immutable command still needs idempotency and authorization when executed; local referential transparency is not an end-to-end transaction guarantee.

    5.3.2 · Domain models, entities, value objects

    An entity has identity across changes; a value object is defined by its value; a domain model expresses meaningful rules. Payment 42 remains the same entity after status changes. Money(USD,100) is a value that should reject incompatible arithmetic or apply an explicit conversion policy. A domain service can coordinate a rule that belongs to no single entity. Avoid an anemic model that scatters every invariant across controllers, while keeping trivial data transport simple.

    5.3.3 · Object collaboration

    An object collaboration describes messages and ownership, not just fields. The checkout orchestrator asks inventory to reserve, asks payments to authorize, and records order state. Neither inventory nor payments should silently mutate the other's private records. Make results explicit so partial failure can be handled. Too much conversational object traffic can become a distributed performance problem if moved across network boundaries; a good in-process collaboration is not automatically a good remote API.

    5.3.4 · Testability and design for change

    Testability follows controllable inputs, visible outcomes, and explicit effects. Inject a fake gateway to test declined-payment behavior without network calls, then test the real adapter against a contract environment. A mock expectation that asserts every internal method call can make refactoring expensive while proving little business behavior. Prefer invariant and outcome tests, and retain integration coverage for transactions, serialization, timeouts, and resource cleanup that a fake cannot faithfully establish.

    Architecture review · Which payment abstractions remain useful if the implementation moves from objects to pure functions?

    Test approved, declined, and uncertain outcomes without real charges. Keep integer units and currency explicit. A test fake validates orchestration only; real serialization, timeouts, and persistence need separate integration evidence. Do not map a timeout to decline simply to make a test pass.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.4

    Design for change, testing & functions

    Prerequisites: 5.3 · Side effects, domain models & collaboration4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Start with a poorly designed payment-processing class. Refactor it into appropriate components, showing which problems each design improvement solves.

    This chapter examines design for change, testing & functions through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    5.4.1 · Refactoring and recognizing code smells

    Refactoring preserves intended behavior while improving structure. Start by characterizing the tangled payment class: valid charge, decline, provider timeout, and persistence failure. Then extract parsing, fee calculation, gateway calls, and storage incrementally. A long method, duplicated conditional, or feature envy is evidence to investigate, not proof that a design pattern is required. Keep tests focused on observable obligations so moving code does not change payment semantics accidentally.

    5.4.2 · Functional programming alternatives to object-centric design

    A functional design can represent payment decisions as pure transformations of values, with effects interpreted at the boundary. decide(state, command) may yield events and requested external actions; an interpreter commits events or calls a gateway. This reduces hidden mutation and makes replaying logic easier. It still needs ownership, durable execution, and effect deduplication. Objects and functions are complementary tools; choose the representation that makes invariants and collaboration clearest in the language and team context.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · injected collaborator

    class RecordingGateway:
    def __init__(self): self.calls = []
    def charge(self, command):
        self.calls.append(command)
        return "uncertain"

def pay(command, gateway):
    return gateway.charge(command)

gateway = RecordingGateway()
assert pay({"amount_minor":100,"currency":"USD"}, gateway) == "uncertain"

    The collaborator is injected and its uncertain result remains explicit. A production service also validates the money and owns persistence and reconciliation; this small function isolates the dependency, not the entire payment system.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.1

    Dependencies, inversion & composition

    Prerequisites: Object-Oriented and Modular Software Design6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines dependencies, inversion & composition through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.1.1 · Dependency, dependency direction, and inversion

    A notification service that imports a concrete email SDK knows both business behavior and infrastructure details. Dependency direction describes that source-level knowledge; inversion makes high-level policy depend on an abstract sending contract that adapters implement. Runtime calls still reach a concrete implementation. Merely moving the SDK constructor into a helper does not invert the dependency if the service still consumes provider-specific types and exceptions. Protect the semantic contract as well as the import graph.

    6.1.2 · Inversion of Control (IoC)

    Inversion of Control means some control is delegated to a framework or external coordinator: an event loop invokes your callback, or a host constructs your request handler. Dependency Injection is one way to supply collaborators under that arrangement, not a synonym for every form of IoC. Registration order, callback lifetime, and failure propagation still need documentation. Giving control to a framework relocates decisions; it does not remove responsibility for them.

    6.1.3 · Dependency Injection (DI)

    Dependency Injection supplies a collaborator rather than constructing or locating it internally. NotificationService(sender) can run with email, SMS, or a recording test sender. The composition root chooses the concrete implementation. DI can be ordinary argument passing; a container is optional. If the caller still supplies one giant object exposing every infrastructure dependency, the design retains broad coupling despite using injection syntax. Keep the contract narrow and its behavior explicit.

    6.1.4 · Constructor, property/setter, and method injection

    Constructor injection makes mandatory dependencies available throughout an object's valid lifetime. Setter injection can model optional or later configuration but risks partially initialized objects. Method injection supplies a collaborator only for one operation and makes per-call variation explicit. Do not store a request-specific dependency passed to a long-lived object unless ownership and concurrency permit it. Select the injection form from required lifetime and validity, rather than assuming framework conventions are universal.

    6.1.5 · Dependency inversion principle vs DI

    Dependency inversion is a design principle about which knowledge depends on which abstraction. DI is a construction technique. A service can receive a concrete SDK through its constructor and still violate the intended abstraction boundary; conversely, a manually wired function can depend on a stable protocol without using a container. Review provider-specific errors, schemas, and resource handles crossing the boundary. Syntax alone cannot prove that high-level policy has been isolated from volatile details.

    6.1.6 · Composition roots and DI containers

    The composition root builds the application graph in one comprehensible place. A DI container automates construction and lifetime resolution; it can detect some invalid graphs but can also hide dependencies and defer errors until runtime. Validate registrations at startup and prefer explicit ownership for disposable resources. For three collaborators, manual construction may be easiest. Use container features when they solve real wiring or integration complexity, not to turn every value into a globally resolvable service.

    Architecture review · How would the ownership rules change if a job outlives both a request scope and a user session?

    Within scope one, a scoped resolution returns A twice; scope two returns B twice. Transients return new identities; a process-owned singleton returns S in both scopes. Add a disposable resource and prove scope end cleans it up. Reject a singleton capturing a request-scoped disposable rather than hiding the bug in a locator.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    For three collaborators, manual construction may be easiest.

    Carry forward: Startup selects implementations · Container or code constructs graph · Validate graph and ownership · Application uses resolved collaborators.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.2

    Lifetimes, ownership & cleanup

    Prerequisites: 6.1 · Dependencies, inversion & composition6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines lifetimes, ownership & cleanup through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.2.1 · Transient, scoped, singleton, and framework-specific lifetimes

    Transient means a resolution creates a new instance; scoped means instances are reused within a defined scope; singleton means reuse within the container or application boundary specified by the framework. None implies global uniqueness across processes. If two request scopes each resolve a scoped unit of work twice, they see identities A,A and B,B. A singleton shared by many requests must meet its concurrency contract. Framework names and disposal rules differ and must be checked.

    6.2.2 · Request scopes, session scopes, and custom scopes

    A request scope lasts for one request, while a session scope can span many requests and hold different privacy or memory risks. Custom job scopes are useful for background processing independent of HTTP. Do not let a job borrow a request-scoped connection after the response has disposed it. Create a job scope with a defined end and propagate only necessary immutable identifiers. A scope is an ownership convention, not automatically a database transaction or authenticated-user boundary.

    6.2.3 · Object creation vs object ownership

    Creation, reference, and ownership are different relationships. A factory may create a connection while the caller owns disposal; a container may create and retain it until scope end. Two components holding a reference must not both assume exclusive closing rights. Write ownership into the contract. Returning a lazily evaluated query from a disposed repository is a common lifetime bug even when the return type matches; materialize bounded data or transfer an explicit streaming owner.

    6.2.4 · Disposal, cleanup, and resource lifecycles

    Cleanup must run on success, failure, and cancellation. Use structured scopes or finally blocks to return pool permits, close streams, and roll back unfinished transactions. Garbage collection is not a timely release guarantee for external resources. Cleanup can itself fail, so preserve the primary failure while recording cleanup problems. Resource lifetimes affect capacity: leaking one database connection per failed request can exhaust a pool even if the healthy request path is fast.

    6.2.5 · Lazy initialization

    Lazy initialization defers creation until the resource is needed. This can avoid unused work, but moves latency and failure to the first caller and introduces a concurrent initialization race. Define whether failed initialization is retried, cached, or surfaced permanently. A lock or runtime lazy primitive must protect publication as required. Warming essential dependencies at startup may provide clearer readiness behavior when accepting traffic without them would immediately fail.

    6.2.6 · Dependency cycles and captive dependencies

    A dependency cycle A→B→A often signals mixed responsibilities or missing coordination; breaking it with a service locator can hide rather than solve the model. A captive dependency occurs when a long-lived owner retains a shorter-lived collaborator, such as a singleton keeping a request's unit of work. Refactor the operation to receive a valid scope or narrow factory. The fix must preserve ownership and authorization context rather than merely satisfy the container's graph validator.

    Architecture review · How would the ownership rules change if a job outlives both a request scope and a user session?

    Within scope one, a scoped resolution returns A twice; scope two returns B twice. Transients return new identities; a process-owned singleton returns S in both scopes. Add a disposable resource and prove scope end cleans it up. Reject a singleton capturing a request-scoped disposable rather than hiding the bug in a locator.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Refactor the operation to receive a valid scope or narrow factory.

    Carry forward: Singleton captures request object · Request ends and disposes object · Later caller uses invalid dependency · Pass a scope-safe operation instead.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.3

    Injection, locators & factories

    Prerequisites: 6.2 · Lifetimes, ownership & cleanup4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines injection, locators & factories through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.3.1 · DI vs service locator

    DI makes collaborators visible in construction or function parameters. A service locator lets code request them from a registry, hiding dependencies behind runtime lookups. Locators can be appropriate at a deliberate integration boundary, but application code that reaches into a global locator is harder to reason about and test. Avoid replacing constructor arguments with one injected container; that often preserves the locator pattern under a different name. Resolve dependencies near the composition boundary.

    6.3.2 · DI vs factory pattern

    A factory encapsulates creation or selection; DI supplies an already selected collaborator or a factory itself. A notification service receiving sender_factory can choose a channel at runtime without importing concrete SDKs. The factory's returned lifetime must be clear: is each sender owned by the caller, shared, or scoped? Do not dispose a shared singleton as though every factory call created a private object. These patterns answer different questions and frequently work together.

    Architecture review · How would the ownership rules change if a job outlives both a request scope and a user session?

    Within scope one, a scoped resolution returns A twice; scope two returns B twice. Transients return new identities; a process-owned singleton returns S in both scopes. Add a disposable resource and prove scope end cleans it up. Reject a singleton capturing a request-scoped disposable rather than hiding the bug in a locator.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    The factory's returned lifetime must be clear: is each sender owned by the caller, shared, or scoped? Do not dispose a shared singleton as though every factory call created a private object.

    Carry forward: Inject channel factory · Select SMS for this command · Factory returns defined-lifetime sender · Caller honors ownership contract.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.4

    Creational patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.3 · Injection, locators & factories6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines creational patterns through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.4.1 · Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton

    Creational patterns organize construction. Factory Method varies creation through a creator operation; Abstract Factory supplies a compatible family; Builder assembles a complex value through explicit steps; Prototype copies a configured instance; Singleton constrains instance access within a specified boundary. They are alternatives only when solving the same construction problem. A simple constructor is better when it already expresses all valid states. Pay particular attention to invalid partial builders, shallow-copy aliases, and global mutable singleton state.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Factory Method

    A creator varies the product it constructs through an overridable or supplied creation operation. A report exporter can ask make_writer() without selecting a concrete writer in its processing skeleton. Use it when construction is a meaningful variation point; a plain injected function is often enough. It differs from Abstract Factory, which creates a compatible family. Avoid inheritance merely to rename a constructor.

    export(rows):
    writer = make_writer()
    writer.write(rows)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Abstract Factory

    A family factory constructs mutually compatible collaborators, such as a renderer and template engine for one notification format. It prevents accidentally mixing incompatible families. It adds interfaces and can make introducing a new product kind expensive. Prefer direct construction when there is one stable family; choose it when clients genuinely switch whole families rather than only one implementation.

    family = HtmlNotificationFactory()
renderer = family.renderer()
template = family.template()
renderer.render(template, data)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Builder

    A builder accumulates a complex construction request and validates it before creating a usable value. A notification can require recipient and template while allowing optional locale and expiry. Do not expose an invalid partially built notification as if ready. A direct constructor or named parameters is clearer for a small value. Unlike a factory family, the builder emphasizes staged assembly and validation.

    builder.to(recipient).template(template_id)
notification = builder.expires_at(deadline).build()
# build rejects missing recipient or incompatible fields
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Prototype

    A prototype creates an object by copying an existing configured instance. Copying a report layout can be convenient when configuration is expensive. Define shallow versus deep copy and ownership of shared resources; copying a connection handle does not create an independent connection. Prefer immutable shared configuration plus new per-request state when that makes aliasing clearer.

    layout = prototype.clone_owned_values()
layout.title = "Monthly report"
# Shared immutable font data remains shared
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Singleton

    A singleton restricts instance access within a specified program or container boundary. It is not globally unique across processes. Shared immutable configuration can be appropriate; shared mutable request state creates races and testing interference. Container-managed singleton lifetime and the classic global-access pattern are related but distinct. Prefer explicit injection and documented ownership so global access does not hide dependencies or prevent isolation.

    configuration = load_immutable_configuration()
service = Service(configuration)
# One application-owned instance; no hidden global lookup
    Architecture review · How would the ownership rules change if a job outlives both a request scope and a user session?

    Within scope one, a scoped resolution returns A twice; scope two returns B twice. Transients return new identities; a process-owned singleton returns S in both scopes. Add a disposable resource and prove scope end cleans it up. Reject a singleton capturing a request-scoped disposable rather than hiding the bug in a locator.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    A simple constructor is better when it already expresses all valid states.

    Carry forward: Need valid object construction · Choose variation or assembly mechanism · Establish ownership and invariants · Avoid unnecessary global state.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.5

    Structural patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.4 · Creational patterns8 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines structural patterns through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.5.1 · Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy

    Structural patterns organize collaboration: Adapter translates an interface; Bridge separates two independently varying dimensions; Composite treats leaves and groups uniformly; Decorator adds behavior around a collaborator; Facade offers a focused entry point; Flyweight shares immutable intrinsic state; Proxy controls access to a target. They do not all mean “wrapper.” Compare the intent and preserved contract. A decorator that retries a non-idempotent charge changes observable semantics and needs more justification than a transparent logging wrapper.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Adapter

    An adapter translates an existing interface or representation into the contract its client needs. A provider-specific SMS response becomes accepted, declined, or uncertain with a stable reference. Translation must preserve meaning, not only field names. Use it at a real interoperability boundary; avoid wrappers that expose the same volatile SDK types. Unlike Decorator, its principal intent is interface translation.

    send(message):
    raw = sdk.submit(encode(message))
    return map_provider_outcome(raw)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Bridge

    A bridge separates two independent dimensions of variation, such as notification content types and delivery transports. Each content model uses a transport contract rather than subclassing every content-channel combination. It costs explicit composition and boundaries. It differs from Adapter, which usually reconciles an existing mismatch; Bridge deliberately designs independent variation before combinations multiply.

    class Receipt:
    constructor(transport): self.transport = transport
    deliver(data): return self.transport.send(format_receipt(data))
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Composite

    A composite exposes a compatible interface for leaves and groups. A notification audience may be a user or a group of audiences. Recursive traversal must define cycles, duplicates, failure aggregation, and size limits. Do not treat a group send as atomically successful just because it shares a method with a leaf. Prefer an ordinary collection loop when a tree-shaped structure does not clarify the domain.

    recipients(node, seen):
    if node.id in seen: return []
    seen.add(node.id)
    return node.users_or_recursive_children(seen)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Decorator

    A decorator preserves a collaborator interface while adding behavior around calls, such as metrics or formatting. Composition order matters: retry(metrics(sender)) counts attempts differently from metrics(retry(sender)). A retry decorator changes effect risk unless operations are safe under a stable identity contract. Use it for orthogonal behavior, not to bury business policy in an opaque stack. Unlike Adapter, it normally retains the same interface.

    send(message):
    start = clock()
    try: return inner.send(message)
    finally: metrics.observe(clock() - start)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Facade

    A facade offers a focused entry point to a subsystem, such as submit_notification() coordinating validation, templating, and durable intent. It reduces the client’s need to understand subsystem details. It must not turn into an unbounded god object or conceal important asynchronous outcomes. Unlike a proxy, its main purpose is a simpler subsystem interface, not controlling access to an otherwise identical target.

    submit(command):
    validated = validate(command)
    return intents.persist(render_plan(validated))
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Flyweight

    A flyweight shares immutable intrinsic state while keeping per-use context external. Many rendered notifications can reuse one parsed template definition while each supplies a recipient and variables. Sharing mutable recipient state would leak data. Measure memory pressure before adding a pool or cache; ordinary immutable reuse can be sufficient. A flyweight does not automatically provide cache invalidation or lifetime management.

    template = parsed_templates.get(version)
output_a = render(template, context_a)
output_b = render(template, context_b)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Proxy

    A proxy implements a target interface while controlling access, placement, or initialization. An authorization proxy can check permission before forwarding a document read. Remote proxies must expose network uncertainty rather than pretending every local call is instant and reliable. Unlike a facade, it commonly stands in for the same conceptual target. Avoid a transparent-looking API that hides expensive retries or unbounded lazy loads.

    read(document_id, actor):
    authorize(actor, document_id)
    return target.read(document_id)
    Architecture review · How would the ownership rules change if a job outlives both a request scope and a user session?

    Within scope one, a scoped resolution returns A twice; scope two returns B twice. Transients return new identities; a process-owned singleton returns S in both scopes. Add a disposable resource and prove scope end cleans it up. Reject a singleton capturing a request-scoped disposable rather than hiding the bug in a locator.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    They do not all mean “wrapper.” Compare the intent and preserved contract.

    Carry forward: Existing collaborator contract · Translate, compose, share or guard · Preserve stated behavior · Account for added calls and state.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.6

    Behavioral patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.5 · Structural patterns11 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines behavioral patterns through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.6.1 · Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor

    Behavioral patterns organize decisions and coordination. Strategy selects interchangeable algorithms; Observer notifies subscribers; Command represents an intention; State varies behavior by lifecycle; Chain routes a request through handlers; Template Method fixes a skeleton with extension points; Iterator traverses; Mediator coordinates; Memento captures recoverable local state; Visitor adds operations over a known structure. Each introduces a particular extension boundary. Choose it when that boundary matches expected change; do not add a pattern merely to name a few conditionals.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Strategy

    A strategy supplies an interchangeable algorithm behind a stable behavioral contract, such as channel selection or fee calculation. It lets one algorithm vary without changing its caller. The strategies must agree on units, errors, and effect semantics. A single stable formula can be a function rather than a class hierarchy. Strategy differs from State because the variation is selected policy rather than lifecycle-dependent behavior.

    price = pricing_strategy.calculate(order)
require(price.currency == order.currency)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Observer

    An observer subscribes to notifications from a subject. Define synchronous versus asynchronous delivery, subscription lifetime, ordering, and exceptions. A local callback list is not a durable broker. A slow or failing observer can delay the subject if invoked inline; an unremoved observer can retain memory. Use for real one-to-many reactions, but use durable event publication when the reaction must survive a process crash.

    for observer in snapshot(subscribers):
    notify_under_defined_failure_policy(observer, event)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Command

    A command represents an intention with explicit inputs and identity, enabling scheduling or audit. It differs from an event, which records a fact already accepted. A retryable command must define duplicate handling and validity at execution time. Capturing an arbitrary closure may retain invalid request resources and cannot automatically be persisted. Prefer serializable domain data and an explicit handler for durable work.

    command = SendReceipt(order_id, operation_id)
handler.handle(command)
# Handler checks current authorization and state
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    State

    State objects or transition tables vary behavior by an entity lifecycle. A pending payment accepts settlement evidence; a refunded payment rejects shipment under the domain policy. Keep transitions and guards explicit and persist them atomically. One class per state is optional; a small transition table may be clearer. Unlike Strategy, current state is constrained by history and cannot be selected arbitrarily by a caller.

    require((payment.state, event.kind) in allowed_transitions)
payment.state = next_state(payment.state, event)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Chain of Responsibility

    A chain passes a request through ordered handlers that may handle, transform, reject, or forward it. Authentication, admission, and parsing middleware are common examples. Define termination and propagation rules so an omitted next() does not silently swallow work. Handler order can change security and cost. It differs from a workflow requiring every mandatory stage to commit; a chain alone supplies no durable progress or compensation.

    auth(rate_limit(parse(application)))(request)
# Each handler has explicit rejection and continuation rules
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Template Method

    A template method fixes an algorithm skeleton and permits selected steps to vary, commonly through inheritance. A base import job can enforce validate, transform, and commit order while formats customize transformation. The base class must preserve valid extension points. Strategy composition is often easier when several steps vary independently. Avoid inheritance that allows subclasses to skip the invariant-protecting skeleton entirely.

    run(input):
    validate(input)
    result = transform(input)
    return commit(result)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Iterator

    An iterator exposes traversal without requiring clients to know the collection representation. Database cursors or paginated readers also carry lifetime, ordering, and resource contracts. A lazy iterator can hold a connection while a slow client waits; disposing its owner too early can break traversal. Define snapshot and mutation behavior. For small bounded results, a materialized list may be simpler and safer.

    with open_bounded_cursor(query) as rows:
    for row in rows:
        consume(row)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Mediator

    A mediator coordinates collaborators that would otherwise communicate through many direct relationships. A checkout coordinator can sequence inventory and payments while each remains focused. The mediator must have explicit state and failure behavior; otherwise it becomes a god object with hidden dependencies. A durable workflow orchestrator is one possible distributed extension, not a guarantee supplied by the object pattern itself.

    reservation = inventory.reserve(command)
outcome = payments.authorize(command.operation_id)
coordinate_outcomes(reservation, outcome)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Memento

    A memento captures state for a supported restoration boundary without exposing arbitrary internals. An editor may snapshot local draft state for undo. Define what is included and whether references are copied safely. Restoring local memory cannot reverse a payment or erase a message already sent. Event history, compensations, and backups solve different problems. Use when state capture is manageable and restoration semantics are genuinely well defined.

    before = draft.snapshot_owned_values()
draft.apply(edit)
draft.restore(before)
# No claim about undoing external effects
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Visitor

    A visitor adds operations over a known structure by dispatching on element type. A document tree can support export, validation, or counting without placing every operation on every node. It eases adding operations but makes adding new element types more expensive because visitors must handle them. Prefer ordinary pattern matching when it is simpler in the language. Keep exhaustive handling and unknown-element behavior explicit during schema evolution.

    visit(node):
    match node.kind:
        case "text": return export_text(node)
        case "image": return export_image(node)
        case _: raise UnsupportedNode
    Architecture review · How would the ownership rules change if a job outlives both a request scope and a user session?

    Within scope one, a scoped resolution returns A twice; scope two returns B twice. Transients return new identities; a process-owned singleton returns S in both scopes. Add a disposable resource and prove scope end cleans it up. Reject a singleton capturing a request-scoped disposable rather than hiding the bug in a locator.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Each introduces a particular extension boundary.

    Carry forward: Behavior varies · Identify the axis of variation · Choose an explicit coordination contract · Compare with direct functions and conditionals.

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.7

    Enterprise patterns & boundaries

    Prerequisites: 6.6 · Behavioral patterns5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Create a notification platform supporting email, SMS, and push notifications. Evolve it from hardcoded classes to DI, Strategy, Factory, and Decorator patterns.

    This chapter examines enterprise patterns & boundaries through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    6.7.1 · Repository, Unit of Work, Specification, CQRS, and dependency boundaries

    Repository mediates domain-oriented access to persistent data; Unit of Work groups changes under one commit decision; Specification represents a reusable predicate; CQRS separates command and query models where their needs justify it. A repository should not pretend remote calls and local transactions share identical failure semantics. A Unit of Work must own its transaction and cleanup. CQRS can be implemented inside one process and one database; event sourcing and independent services are optional additional choices.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Repository

    A repository mediates domain-oriented persistence rather than exposing storage syntax everywhere. Its contract must define transactions, errors, query bounds, and returned-value lifetime. A repository per table is not always the right aggregate boundary. Do not hide slow remote calls or lazy resources behind a misleadingly cheap-looking method. Use it when it protects meaningful knowledge, while retaining real storage integration tests.

    reservation = repository.get_for_update(reservation_id)
reservation.confirm(payment_evidence)
repository.save(reservation)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Unit of Work

    A Unit of Work groups local changes under one commit and tracks their ownership. Inventory decrement and reservation insert can belong to one transaction. Commit and cleanup semantics must be explicit, and collaborators must not secretly commit independently. It cannot atomically include an unrelated payment provider simply because both are called inside a language scope. Keep the unit short and free of unnecessary network waits.

    with unit_of_work() as uow:
    uow.inventory.reserve(seat)
    uow.reservations.add(record)
    uow.commit()
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Specification

    A specification names a reusable predicate or selection rule, such as eligible_for_refund(payment,now). Keep its semantics explicit when translating it into a database query, especially around nulls, time, and authorization. Reusing a pure predicate is simple; an elaborate expression framework is justified only by real composition needs. A specification describes eligibility, not the atomic transition that prevents eligibility from changing concurrently.

    eligible = RefundPolicy.satisfied_by(payment, now)
if eligible:
    repository.refund_if_still_eligible(payment.version)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    CQRS

    Separate command and query models when they need different behavior or shape. A transaction-safe payment aggregate can emit changes to a read-friendly statement view. The read side can lag, so freshness and rebuilding must be specified. It need not use separate processes, storage engines, or event sourcing. Avoid the additional synchronization and model maintenance when one straightforward model already serves the workload.

    commands.capture(payment_id, operation_id)
statement = queries.account_statement(account_id)
# Projection lag is part of the query contract

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · lifetime identities

    singleton = object()
def new_scope(): return {"scoped": object()}
a, b = new_scope(), new_scope()
assert a["scoped"] is a["scoped"]
assert a["scoped"] is not b["scoped"]
assert object() is not object()
assert singleton is singleton

    The identities model one process. Actual containers differ in registration, disposal, and scope behavior. A real request scope must clean up owned resources; storing its object in a singleton changes the lifetime and can be invalid.

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.1

    Layers, monoliths & ports

    Prerequisites: Object-Oriented and Modular Software Design, Design Patterns, Dependency Injection, and Object Lifecycles6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an online shopping application first as a modular monolith, then examine the conditions under which selected domains should become independent services.

    This chapter examines layers, monoliths & ports through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    7.1.1 · Layered/N-tier architecture

    Layered architecture separates presentation, application behavior, domain policy, and infrastructure at a chosen granularity. Dependencies should be intentional: a controller should not bypass a domain invariant merely because an SQL helper is nearby. Layers can run in one process; physical N-tier deployment is a separate decision. Avoid mandatory pass-through classes that add no policy or abstraction. Trace one change, such as a new pricing rule, to verify that the layer boundary actually localizes knowledge.

    7.1.2 · Modular monoliths

    A modular monolith is deployed as a unit while its modules maintain explicit boundaries and ownership. Orders, catalog, and payments can have separate interfaces and schema ownership in one application. This keeps local calls and coordinated deployment simple while retaining future extraction options. Shared tables writable by every module defeat much of the benefit. Enforce module dependencies in code review or automated checks, and make cross-module operations pass through agreed contracts.

    7.1.3 · Monolith vs microservices

    Microservices add independently deployable processes and data ownership boundaries, along with network failures, version skew, and distributed operations. A monolith can be modular; a set of services can be tightly coupled. Extract inventory when independent scaling, failure isolation, or team ownership gives a concrete benefit. If every change requires simultaneous deployment of five services, independence is mostly nominal. Compare operational cost and transaction complexity against the change that motivated extraction.

    7.1.4 · Clean Architecture

    Clean Architecture places business policy inside dependencies on application-owned abstractions; framework and storage details depend inward. The drawing's circles describe source dependency rules, not the physical path of runtime messages. A use case might call an injected repository implemented by an outer adapter. Avoid leaking ORM entities or HTTP response types into core policy. The cost is extra mapping and contracts; a small CRUD tool may need only a modest version of the same separation.

    7.1.5 · Hexagonal/Ports and Adapters

    Hexagonal architecture names inbound and outbound ports with adapters around the application. A CLI and HTTP controller can invoke the same create-order port; an SQL repository and test fake implement a storage port. Ports express the application's needs rather than every operation a vendor SDK offers. Network isolation is not implied by the hexagon. Test the core with controlled adapters and separately verify serialization, transaction behavior, and failures at real boundaries.

    7.1.6 · Onion Architecture

    Onion Architecture also emphasizes dependencies toward domain policy, often organizing domain, application services, and infrastructure as concentric responsibilities. Names and layer placement vary across communities. Do not argue that one diagram guarantees better design than another with equivalent obligations. Ask whether the order rules can run independently of the web framework and whether storage errors remain explicit. Architectural styles are organizing tools; the concrete contracts and change behavior determine their usefulness.

    Architecture review · Which evidence would justify extracting payments from a modular monolith while retaining the same business invariants?

    Let orders request a payment through a contract; disallow direct imports of the payment storage adapter or writes to its private table. A test should enforce a meaningful dependency rule rather than every incidental class name. Show how a provider adapter can change while the order rule remains stable.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Ask whether the order rules can run independently of the web framework and whether storage errors remain explicit.

    Carry forward: Domain rule · Application coordination · Infrastructure implementation · Dependencies preserve policy independence.

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.2

    Model a bounded context

    Prerequisites: 7.1 · Layers, monoliths & ports4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an online shopping application first as a modular monolith, then examine the conditions under which selected domains should become independent services.

    This chapter examines model a bounded context through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    7.2.1 · Domain-Driven Design (DDD)

    Domain-Driven Design builds a shared model of a complex business with domain experts. Its value is making ambiguous concepts and invariants explicit, not turning every database row into a class. In shopping, “available inventory” may differ between merchandising and reservation processing. Explore those meanings before choosing service boundaries. For a simple reference table, elaborate aggregates and events may cost more than they clarify; apply modeling effort where business behavior is genuinely complex.

    7.2.2 · Bounded contexts and ubiquitous language

    A bounded context defines where a particular model and vocabulary are valid. The catalog's Product can emphasize description and merchandising; fulfillment's Item can emphasize a physical unit and location. Translating between them is deliberate, not evidence that one universal Product schema is missing. Ubiquitous language means consistent domain language inside a context, not forcing every team to use one model. Map interactions and ownership before deciding whether a context is a separate process.

    7.2.3 · Aggregates, entities, value objects, domain services

    An aggregate is a consistency boundary whose root controls changes to its members. An Order might protect the relationship between line items and total amount within a transaction. Entities carry identity; value objects represent interchangeable values; domain services express rules spanning concepts. A huge aggregate containing the entire shop creates contention and awkward loading. Keep invariants that must change atomically together, and handle cross-aggregate coordination explicitly rather than assuming object references imply distributed transactions.

    7.2.4 · Domain events

    A domain event records a meaningful fact such as OrderPlaced, not a vague instruction to “do something.” Include stable identity, time semantics, and enough versioned information for intended consumers without exposing every internal field. Recording an event in memory is not reliable publication. If state and publication intent must agree, persist them atomically through an outbox or another justified mechanism. Consumers must still handle duplicates, delayed delivery, and compatible schema evolution.

    Architecture review · Which evidence would justify extracting payments from a modular monolith while retaining the same business invariants?

    Let orders request a payment through a contract; disallow direct imports of the payment storage adapter or writes to its private table. A test should enforce a meaningful dependency rule rather than every incidental class name. Show how a provider adapter can change while the order rule remains stable.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    If state and publication intent must agree, persist them atomically through an outbox or another justified mechanism.

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.3

    Keep business policy inside

    Prerequisites: 7.2 · Model a bounded context5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an online shopping application first as a modular monolith, then examine the conditions under which selected domains should become independent services.

    This chapter examines keep business policy inside through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    7.3.1 · Dependency rules and module boundaries

    Dependency rules constrain which modules can know about others. A payments module should expose a payment contract rather than allow orders to update its tables directly. Enforce these rules with import boundaries, schema permissions, and architecture tests where useful. Cycles often reveal unclear coordination. A shared utility can become a disguised common domain dependency; prefer explicit data translations when two contexts deliberately have different meanings for apparently similar concepts.

    7.3.2 · Business logic vs orchestration vs infrastructure

    Business logic determines allowed outcomes, orchestration sequences collaborators, and infrastructure performs technical effects. “A refunded order cannot ship” is business logic; coordinating a refund request and status update is orchestration; calling the provider is infrastructure. One function may initially perform all three, but naming the distinctions reveals where tests and failure handling belong. Do not move a business rule into a message broker configuration merely because orchestration happens to be asynchronous.

    7.3.3 · Controllers, services, repositories, adapters

    Controllers translate transport, services coordinate application behavior, repositories mediate data, and adapters implement boundary protocols. These roles are conventions, not mandatory suffixes on class names. An application service can be a function. A domain service has a different purpose from a network-deployed service. Review behavior rather than the directory tree: if a controller owns transaction retries and pricing rules, creating a services folder has not actually separated responsibilities.

    7.3.4 · Anti-corruption layers

    An anti-corruption layer translates a foreign model into the local model so external terminology and quirks do not spread. A legacy provider may call a pending authorization “settled”; the payment context must translate that carefully instead of accepting the label as its own settlement state. The layer adds mappings and reconciliation work. Preserve unmapped states explicitly and fail safely rather than silently coercing every unknown value into success.

    7.3.5 · Event-driven architecture

    Event-driven architecture connects components through events with independent processing. It reduces synchronous coupling in some paths while creating temporal coupling, replay, ordering, and observability obligations. An order can become accepted before a receipt is delivered, but inventory and payment requirements still determine which steps can be deferred. A broker does not supply end-to-end business reliability automatically. Make event ownership, deduplication, persistence, and reconciliation part of the architecture, not an afterthought.

    Architecture review · Which evidence would justify extracting payments from a modular monolith while retaining the same business invariants?

    Let orders request a payment through a contract; disallow direct imports of the payment storage adapter or writes to its private table. A test should enforce a meaningful dependency rule rather than every incidental class name. Show how a provider adapter can change while the order rule remains stable.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    A broker does not supply end-to-end business reliability automatically.

    Carry forward: Durable order event · Broker stores or routes message · Consumer updates its state · Reconciliation detects incomplete outcomes.

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.4

    Evolution without a distributed monolith

    Prerequisites: 7.3 · Keep business policy inside5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an online shopping application first as a modular monolith, then examine the conditions under which selected domains should become independent services.

    This chapter examines evolution without a distributed monolith through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    7.4.1 · Serverless and function-oriented architectures

    Serverless functions can provide managed invocation and elastic execution, but do not remove systems design. Time limits, cold starts, concurrency caps, retries, identity, and durable state all affect behavior. Keep function-local memory as an optimization unless the platform explicitly guarantees more. A function processing a payment event must deduplicate effects across retries. Function-oriented organization can fit small independently triggered tasks; long workflows usually need an explicit durable state owner or workflow engine.

    7.4.2 · Evolutionary architecture

    Evolutionary architecture changes in response to evidence while protecting important properties. Add fitness checks for module boundaries, migration compatibility, latency budgets, or tenant isolation so frequent changes do not silently erode them. A check must express a useful property rather than freeze incidental implementation. An ADR records why a boundary exists and what observation should trigger reconsideration. Evolution is not constant rewriting; many successful changes remove complexity rather than introduce another platform.

    7.4.3 · Technical vs business boundaries

    Technical boundaries group by mechanism, such as controllers or databases; business boundaries group coherent capabilities, such as orders or fulfillment. Both can coexist at different levels. Splitting a company into an “SQL service” and “validation service” often makes every business change cross the network. Start with ownership of decisions and data, then choose internal technical layers. A bounded context is a modeling boundary; it is not automatically equivalent to a team, repository, or deployed service.

    7.4.4 · Distributed monolith antipattern

    A distributed monolith has several processes but little independent change or operation. Symptoms include synchronous chains for every action, shared writable schemas, coordinated releases, and failures cascading across services. Moving calls onto a network without clarifying ownership makes debugging harder and adds partial failure. Consolidating unstable boundaries into a modular deployment can be an improvement. Alternatively, redesign contracts, data ownership, and asynchronous coordination before claiming independent services have been achieved.

    7.4.5 · When not to use microservices

    Avoid microservices when the domain is still changing rapidly, the team cannot operate independent services safely, or scale and isolation do not require them. A modular monolith with measured bottlenecks and tested backups can be a stronger starting point. This is not a claim that microservices are inherently wrong: stable capabilities with distinct traffic and ownership can justify them. Evaluate the complete cost of transactions, deployment, telemetry, security, and incident response before extraction.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Pseudocode · module contract

    place_order(command):
    priced = catalog.quote(command.items)
    reservation = inventory.reserve(command.items)
    payment = payments.authorize(command.operation_id, priced.total)
    return orders.record_outcomes(priced, reservation, payment)
# Modules expose contracts; they do not update each other's private tables.

    This orchestration does not make three remote services one atomic transaction. In a modular monolith some local updates may share a deliberately owned transaction; external effects still need a workflow and reconciliation.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY
