    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.1

    Model resources and messages

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design, Networking Foundations for System Design6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a payment API with create-payment, payment-status, refunds, idempotency protection, duplicate requests, and failed network responses.

    This chapter examines model resources and messages through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    8.1.1 · API fundamentals and interface contracts

    An API is a communication contract, including inputs, outputs, side effects, error semantics, identity, deadlines, and compatibility. For create-payment, specify integer minor units and currency, distinguish a declined payment from an uncertain transport outcome, and identify who may access its status. A schema alone cannot describe whether a repeated request charges twice. Write example success, validation failure, duplicate, and lost-response histories before selecting a transport framework.

    8.1.2 · REST, GraphQL, gRPC, RPC

    REST organizes resource-oriented interactions using HTTP semantics; GraphQL exposes a typed query graph; gRPC commonly offers schema-defined RPC with streaming; RPC generally models operations. None is inherently correct for every boundary. GraphQL can reduce over-fetching but needs query-cost control and field authorization. RPC can make domain actions clear but still needs compatibility and retry semantics. Compare client needs, caching, tooling, latency, and evolution using the same operation, not only request syntax.

    8.1.3 · Resource modeling

    Resources should reflect stable business identities. POST /payments creates an operation; GET /payments/{id} reports its state; POST /payments/{id}/refunds creates a separately tracked refund. Hiding every action under one generic /execute endpoint loses useful semantics, but forcing every domain action into CRUD can also obscure behavior. A refund resource needs its own amount, authorization, idempotency identity, and lifecycle. Use ownership and state transitions to guide the model.

    8.1.4 · Request/response schemas

    Validate structural shape and business meaning separately. A syntactically valid amount of −100 may violate the payment operation; an unknown field can be ignored or rejected according to compatibility policy. Bound payload size, collection lengths, and accepted encodings before expensive processing. Return machine-readable error codes with safe messages and a request identifier. Do not echo secrets or provider internals in validation errors. Schema evolution must consider clients that deserialize strictly as well as those that ignore extensions.

    8.1.5 · Status codes and error models

    HTTP status codes describe the protocol outcome, while an operation body may describe asynchronous business state. 201 can identify a created payment resource that is still pending; 202 means accepted for processing, not financially approved. A timeout has no definitive business meaning. Use stable application codes for validation, conflict, authorization, and retry advice. Do not translate every provider error into a generic 500 if clients need to distinguish a correctable request from an uncertain submitted operation.

    8.1.6 · Pagination, filtering, sorting

    Pagination bounds work and response size. Define stable sorting, tie-breakers, allowed filters, maximum page size, and authorization at the query boundary. Returning “all payments” can exhaust memory and expose data even when the endpoint looks simple. Sorting by created_at alone is ambiguous for equal timestamps; append a unique identifier. Offset and cursor approaches differ under concurrent insertion, and neither automatically guarantees a consistent snapshot of a changing collection.

    Architecture review · Can a public API offer a permanent idempotency promise with finite storage? Define a defensible contract.

    Use keyset_page() for ordered pairs and test insertion before a page boundary. For idempotency, bind actor, key, fingerprint, state, and result atomically; reject a mismatched payload. A plain dictionary checked before a separate insert does not protect concurrent requests or restart recovery.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Sorting by created_at alone is ambiguous for equal timestamps; append a unique identifier.

    Carry forward: Filter authorized records · Sort by time then unique ID · Apply bounded page size · Return continuation metadata.

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.2

    Compatibility & idempotency

    Prerequisites: 8.1 · Model resources and messages4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a payment API with create-payment, payment-status, refunds, idempotency protection, duplicate requests, and failed network responses.

    This chapter examines compatibility & idempotency through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    8.2.1 · Cursor vs offset pagination

    Offset pagination skips a number of rows and is easy to express, but inserts before the offset can create duplicates or omissions between pages. Keyset cursors encode the last ordered key, such as (created_at,id), to continue after that position. They avoid some skip cost and shift anomalies but still need a consistency contract for changing rows. Sign or validate opaque cursors and bind them to the applicable filters and tenant context.

    8.2.2 · API versioning and compatibility

    Compatible evolution preserves supported client behavior. Adding an optional field may be safe for tolerant clients but break strict validators or exhaustive enum handling. Changing an amount from minor to major units is breaking even if its type remains numeric. Use versioned semantics, overlap windows, telemetry on old consumers, and contract tests. A new URL version is only one technique; it does not remove the obligation to migrate clients and preserve stored event interpretation.

    8.2.3 · Idempotency and idempotency keys

    An idempotency key identifies one logical operation across attempts. Store its owner, request fingerprint, execution state, and committed result under a uniqueness and atomicity rule. The same key with a different payload must conflict. If the provider may have charged before a timeout, use its stable operation key or reconcile before resubmitting. Retention and key reuse rules matter. Local deduplication does not provide exactly-once external execution across an uncooperative provider boundary.

    Architecture review · Can a public API offer a permanent idempotency promise with finite storage? Define a defensible contract.

    Use keyset_page() for ordered pairs and test insertion before a page boundary. For idempotency, bind actor, key, fingerprint, state, and result atomically; reject a mismatched payload. A plain dictionary checked before a separate insert does not protect concurrent requests or restart recovery.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Retention and key reuse rules matter.

    Carry forward: Key K and payload hash H · Atomically reserve operation K · Execute or reconcile provider operation · Persist and replay the same result.

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.3

    Control access, load & long operations

    Prerequisites: 8.2 · Compatibility & idempotency5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a payment API with create-payment, payment-status, refunds, idempotency protection, duplicate requests, and failed network responses.

    This chapter examines control access, load & long operations through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    8.3.1 · Authentication vs authorization at API boundaries

    Authentication establishes the caller's identity under a trust model; authorization decides whether that caller may perform this operation on this resource. Derive tenant context from authenticated membership, not a freely supplied tenant_id alone. GET /payments/42 must check resource ownership even if payment identifiers are hard to guess. Coarse gateway checks complement, rather than replace, domain authorization. Validate service-to-service credentials as well as user credentials when requests cross internal boundaries.

    8.3.2 · Rate limits and quotas

    A rate limit controls request pace; a quota limits accumulated use over a period or resource dimension. A payment API might limit expensive validation attempts and separately cap daily exports. Define keys, windows, burst behavior, retry advice, and failure policy. One global limit can let a noisy tenant harm everyone, while per-user limits can miss coordinated abuse. Distributed enforcement needs atomic state or an explicit approximation and regional allocation contract.

    8.3.3 · Retries and timeouts

    Retries should fit an overall deadline and target transient, safe-to-repeat work. Budget time for connection acquisition, attempts, and backoff; propagate remaining time downstream. Exponential backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retries but does not create capacity. Avoid retries independently at every layer: three attempts at each of four layers can amplify one intent into 81 attempts. For side effects, retries need stable identity and reconciliation of uncertain outcomes.

    8.3.4 · Streaming APIs and long-running operations

    A long-running operation can return an operation resource and let clients poll or subscribe for progress. Streaming returns a sequence with explicit framing, cancellation, buffering, and resume policy. A disconnected client does not necessarily cancel the business job; define who owns it after submission. Persist required job state outside request-local memory. Avoid holding a database transaction open for the lifetime of a slow stream; read bounded pages or transfer a deliberate streaming resource owner.

    8.3.5 · Webhooks and delivery acknowledgments

    A webhook is an asynchronous request to another party. Sign it, include a stable event identifier and timestamp policy, and accept acknowledgments according to a documented delivery contract. A receiver should commit its inbox or effect before acknowledging if persistence is required. A sender can retry a lost acknowledgment, so consumers must deduplicate. A 2xx response proves only what the receiving contract promises, not that every downstream business task has completed.

    Architecture review · Can a public API offer a permanent idempotency promise with finite storage? Define a defensible contract.

    Use keyset_page() for ordered pairs and test insertion before a page boundary. For idempotency, bind actor, key, fingerprint, state, and result atomically; reject a mismatched payload. A plain dictionary checked before a separate insert does not protect concurrent requests or restart recovery.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.4

    Evolve a public contract

    Prerequisites: 8.3 · Control access, load & long operations5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a payment API with create-payment, payment-status, refunds, idempotency protection, duplicate requests, and failed network responses.

    This chapter examines evolve a public contract through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    8.4.1 · Schema evolution

    Schema evolution applies to stored data and events as well as synchronous APIs. Preserve meanings, defaults, field identity, and unknown-value behavior. A consumer replaying a year of events may encounter every historical version, so deleting a decoder can break recovery even if current traffic looks healthy. Use explicit versions or upcasters with tested historical samples. An additive field is not harmless if it changes a signature calculation, a uniqueness rule, or a required business decision.

    8.4.2 · Consumer-driven contracts

    Consumer-driven contracts record assumptions that real consumers make about a provider. Run provider verification against those contracts before release, while also testing behavior that schemas miss. A fixture asserting that status is a string does not protect a client that assumes every returned status is final. Contracts can become brittle if they freeze irrelevant formatting. Focus on observable obligations and maintain representative error, authorization, pagination, and retry scenarios alongside success examples.

    8.4.3 · API gateways and BFF

    A gateway provides shared edge concerns; a Backend for Frontend adapts APIs for a particular client experience. A mobile BFF can aggregate necessary data and reduce chatty requests, but adds latency, capacity, and ownership concerns. Keep resource-level authorization in the systems that understand ownership. Avoid a universal aggregation service that every product must change together. Cache only representations whose key, identity scope, and freshness policy are well defined.

    8.4.4 · Public vs internal APIs

    An internal API still crosses a trust, version, or failure boundary. Internal clients may have different release schedules and can send malformed or excessive requests. A public API generally needs stronger compatibility commitments, discoverability, abuse control, and support processes, but internal status does not justify skipping authentication or invariants. Document audience and lifetime explicitly. A service initially called “private” often becomes a dependency whose accidental behavior is difficult to change.

    8.4.5 · API documentation and discoverability

    Documentation should explain complete operation histories: request examples, errors, authorization, pagination, timeouts, idempotency, and asynchronous status. Machine-readable schemas help generate clients, while prose defines semantics those schemas cannot express. A runnable sandbox must distinguish simulated effects from real charges. Track documentation versions with implementation, and test key examples. Discoverability is practical: users should know how to find the right operation, determine its scope, and recover when the happy path fails.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · keyset continuation

    from mechanisms import keyset_page
rows = [(1,1,"A"), (1,2,"B"), (2,3,"C")]
assert keyset_page(rows, after=(1,1)) == rows[1:]

    The ordered pair supplies a stable tie-breaker. A real cursor also needs query and tenant binding, validation, and a defined consistency policy. Keyset pagination does not create a snapshot of a changing dataset.

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.1

    Storage promises & database families

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design9 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Choose storage technologies for user profiles, financial transactions, chat messages, event logs, and uploaded PDFs. Justify each decision.

    This chapter examines storage promises & database families through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    9.1.1 · What data storage must guarantee

    Storage choices begin with promises: what is accepted, when it is committed, how it can be read, and which failures it survives. A chat history, an audit ledger, and a thumbnail cache need different retention and correctness contracts. Name the authoritative copy and recovery procedure. A database label alone does not establish transactions, isolation, backups, or acknowledgment durability; these depend on configuration and usage. Choose by access patterns and invariants before comparing product features.

    9.1.2 · Relational databases and SQL

    A relational model represents facts as relations with keys and constraints; SQL expresses queries and changes over that model. Foreign keys and transactions can protect relationships when configured and used appropriately. A ledger benefits from explicit account and entry relationships and atomic updates. Joins are not inherently a scaling failure; indexes, cardinality, workload, and execution plans matter. Start normalized for ownership and invariants, then denormalize specific read paths when evidence justifies maintenance cost.

    9.1.3 · Document databases

    A document database groups nested data under a document identity and commonly permits flexible structures. A user profile with preferences may fit a document aggregate well. Flexibility moves some validation and migration responsibility into schema conventions and application code; it does not make schema disappear. Decide whether updates across documents need atomicity, how nested collections grow, and which fields are indexed. An unbounded array of all chat messages in one user document is usually a poor ownership and growth boundary.

    9.1.4 · Key-value databases

    A key-value store maps keys to values under a defined read/write contract. It suits sessions, cached objects, or direct ID lookup when operations match the key design. Querying arbitrary value fields may require secondary structures maintained separately. Do not assume all key-value stores share durability or consistency behavior. A key such as tenant:42:session:7 should encode the required identity scope, while expiration and invalidation determine whether the value remains usable after permissions change.

    9.1.5 · Wide-column stores

    Wide-column systems organize data around partition keys and ordered clustering dimensions in common implementations. A conversation partition with messages ordered by sequence can support bounded history reads. Partition size and hot-key traffic must be planned: one enormous room can concentrate load despite a large cluster. Model queries first, duplicate data deliberately for other access patterns, and document which constraints or joins the application must enforce. The category is not a universal guarantee about every implementation.

    9.1.6 · Graph databases

    Graph storage makes relationships and traversals first-class, useful when variable-depth relationships are central to queries. Fraud investigation may traverse accounts, devices, and transfers. A relational schema can also represent edges, so compare actual query complexity and locality rather than assuming graph databases alone can model relationships. Bound traversal depth and fan-out, enforce tenant or privacy boundaries during expansion, and inspect the cost of high-degree nodes. An unrestricted traversal can become an expensive data-exfiltration path.

    9.1.7 · Time-series databases

    Time-series data combines timestamps, measurements, and dimensions. Storage can exploit time locality, compression, partitioning, and retention. Device metrics with bounded labels fit this model, while adding a unique request ID as a metric label can explode cardinality. Decide handling for late data, clock skew, downsampling, and corrections. Time ordering by a device clock is not automatically causal ordering; keep ingestion time or sequence metadata when the distinction matters for investigation.

    9.1.8 · Search indexes

    A search index stores representations optimized for retrieval rather than primary transactional ownership. An inverted index maps terms to postings; document scores and filters produce ranked results. Updates commonly propagate asynchronously from an authoritative store, so search may lag or temporarily retain deleted content. Authorization filtering must remain correct despite that lag. Keep enough source identity and version information to rebuild the index and reject stale updates; treating the index as the only copy makes recovery fragile.

    9.1.9 · Vector indexes: introductory architecture only

    A vector index supports similarity search over numerical embeddings. It typically combines a vector representation, an approximate candidate structure, and metadata filtering. Candidate recall, update cost, memory, distance function, and authorization affect the architecture. An embedding is a derived representation, not an authoritative replacement for a document. Preserve source versions and rebuild paths; approximate retrieval can miss relevant items, and a vector score does not prove a factual answer or permission to expose the source.

    Architecture review · How does restoration from a historical backup interact with current privacy deletion and derived indexes?

    Justify each choice through point reads, ranges, invariants, retention, and byte size. Do not choose five engines merely to cover a taxonomy. Separate PDF bytes from metadata and preserve recoverable references; explain which derived stores can be rebuilt and which facts must remain authoritative.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    An embedding is a derived representation, not an authoritative replacement for a document.

    Carry forward: Source and embedding version · Candidate vector search · Metadata and permission filter · Fetch authoritative source evidence.

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.2

    Files, objects & analytical layouts

    Prerequisites: 9.1 · Storage promises & database families4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Choose storage technologies for user profiles, financial transactions, chat messages, event logs, and uploaded PDFs. Justify each decision.

    This chapter examines files, objects & analytical layouts through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    9.2.1 · Object storage vs block vs file storage

    Object storage exposes named blobs and metadata; block storage exposes addressable blocks; file storage exposes a filesystem namespace and file operations. Uploaded PDFs usually fit object storage plus relational metadata, while a database engine may need a block-backed filesystem with appropriate durability semantics. Protocol and implementation guarantees differ. A URL to an object is not the same as a committed metadata reference: incomplete uploads, orphan objects, and deletion require an explicit lifecycle protocol.

    9.2.2 · OLTP vs OLAP

    OLTP emphasizes many short transactions over current operational state; OLAP emphasizes analytical scans and aggregation over larger histories. Running an unbounded dashboard query on the purchase database can compete with checkout for I/O and memory. Replicating or transforming operational data into analytical storage separates access patterns but creates freshness, lineage, and reconciliation obligations. A single engine can support mixed workloads to a point; measure interference before adding another system solely because two labels exist.

    9.2.3 · Row-oriented vs column-oriented storage

    Row layouts keep fields of a record together; column layouts keep a field's values together across many records. Fetching one customer's complete operational record often favors row-oriented access, while summing revenue across millions of rows can benefit from reading only relevant columns and compression. Modern engines mix techniques, so compare the actual plan. Layout choice affects writes, updates, locality, and compression; it does not replace indexing or a sound logical model.

    9.2.4 · Normalization vs denormalization

    Normalization avoids redundant facts and update anomalies; denormalization deliberately stores derived or repeated data to serve a read path. Store a customer's address once for their current profile, but retain the historical shipping address on a completed order as part of that order's fact. Not all duplication is an error. When a feed stores a cached author name, define whether it is a snapshot or a copy to maintain; ambiguity creates stale-data bugs.

    Architecture review · How does restoration from a historical backup interact with current privacy deletion and derived indexes?

    Justify each choice through point reads, ranges, invariants, retention, and byte size. Do not choose five engines merely to cover a taxonomy. Separate PDF bytes from metadata and preserve recoverable references; explain which derived stores can be rebuilt and which facts must remain authoritative.

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.3

    Model relationships and ownership

    Prerequisites: 9.2 · Files, objects & analytical layouts4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Choose storage technologies for user profiles, financial transactions, chat messages, event logs, and uploaded PDFs. Justify each decision.

    This chapter examines model relationships and ownership through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    9.3.1 · ER diagrams and relational modeling

    An ER model identifies entities, relationships, cardinalities, and constraints. Orders have many lines; each line refers to a product identity and stores purchase-time values needed historically. A diagram should distinguish mandatory from optional relationships and name keys. The model must address deletion and lifecycle: removing a product must not erase a completed order's financial meaning. A schema is an executable part of the design when its constraints enforce the intended relationships.

    9.3.2 · Referential integrity

    Referential integrity ensures a stored relationship refers to an allowed target under the chosen constraint. A foreign key can prevent an order line from referencing a missing order in a relational database. Cascading deletion is a policy decision, not automatically the right cleanup. Across separately owned services, a local foreign key cannot enforce remote existence; use explicit contracts, stable identifiers, events, and reconciliation. Application checks before insertion can race unless protected by an appropriate atomic mechanism.

    9.3.3 · Data ownership

    Data ownership names who may define and change a fact. Payments owns financial outcome records; analytics consumes a derived copy. If several services directly update one table, transaction behavior and release coupling become shared even if their code repositories are separate. Publish contracts for reading and changing owned data, and give consumers the least privilege required. Ownership includes retention, incident response, schema evolution, and recovery, not only the right to create a table.

    9.3.4 · Choosing storage based on access patterns

    Choose storage by the operations and invariants it must support. Profiles may fit relational or document storage; financial entries benefit from transaction and audit constraints; chat history needs conversation/time access; event logs need ordered append and replay; PDFs need large immutable-byte handling. These are workload arguments, not mandatory product assignments. Prefer fewer systems until a measured access pattern justifies another. Every new engine adds backup, security, migration, telemetry, and operational expertise requirements.

    Architecture review · How does restoration from a historical backup interact with current privacy deletion and derived indexes?

    Justify each choice through point reads, ranges, invariants, retention, and byte size. Do not choose five engines merely to cover a taxonomy. Separate PDF bytes from metadata and preserve recoverable references; explain which derived stores can be rebuilt and which facts must remain authoritative.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Prefer fewer systems until a measured access pattern justifies another.

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.4

    Access patterns, retention & operational cost

    Prerequisites: 9.3 · Model relationships and ownership4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Choose storage technologies for user profiles, financial transactions, chat messages, event logs, and uploaded PDFs. Justify each decision.

    This chapter examines access patterns, retention & operational cost through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    9.4.1 · Data retention and lifecycle

    Retention is an explicit lifecycle, not a scheduled delete statement added at the end. Decide legal and business purpose, expiration, archival, backup behavior, and derived-copy deletion. Dropping old partitions may be efficient for time-bounded data, while per-user deletion needs identity-aware propagation. A tombstone may prevent reappearance during replay but still retain personal data; minimize it appropriately. Verify that recovery from an old backup reapplies required deletion decisions instead of resurrecting removed records.

    9.4.2 · Polyglot persistence and its operational costs

    Polyglot persistence gives different workloads suitable engines at the cost of more operating boundaries. A shop might add search only after relational queries fail its relevance or latency needs. It then must track indexing lag, rebuilds, schemas, permissions, and recovery across both stores. Cross-store operations are not one transaction by default. Compare the added capability with total ownership cost, and keep authoritative data and derived representations distinguishable in every diagram and runbook.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Pseudocode · bytes and metadata

    upload = create_authorized_upload(tenant, expected_size)
object = store_and_verify_bytes(upload)
with transaction():
    insert_document(tenant, object.version, object.digest)
    insert_processing_intent(object.version)
# Orphan-byte cleanup handles incomplete metadata handoff.

    The authoritative metadata references a verified immutable byte version. If metadata commit fails, cleanup reconciles orphan objects. Do not claim one local transaction atomically contains a separate object-storage upload.

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.1

    Pages, indexes & query plans

    Prerequisites: Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Data Models and Storage Technologies6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two users attempt to purchase the last available ticket. Demonstrate the lost-update race, show why naive reads fail, and implement valid alternatives using transactions and concurrency control.

    This chapter examines pages, indexes & query plans through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    10.1.1 · How databases store and retrieve records

    A database translates logical records into physical structures and coordinates access while preserving its promises. A lookup may consult an index, fetch pages into memory, inspect visibility, and return a row. The operating system and device still affect latency and durability. Understanding this path explains why one query may be CPU-bound while another waits on I/O. Start by measuring the plan and resource behavior; changing a database category without identifying the expensive step is guesswork.

    10.1.2 · Pages, records, indexes, and buffer pools

    A page is a fixed-size storage unit in many engines; records occupy pages; indexes point toward searchable values or records; a buffer pool caches useful pages. A cache hit avoids some storage I/O but still incurs parsing, execution, and synchronization. If a query touches a million scattered pages, extra application servers may only increase random reads. Working-set size and locality explain performance better than raw table row count alone. Exact page layouts and buffer policies are implementation-specific.

    10.1.3 · B-tree/B+tree and hash indexing

    B-tree families maintain ordered keys with bounded-height traversal; B+tree designs commonly keep data or record references in leaves linked for range scans. Hash indexing suits equality under its implementation but does not provide ordered range traversal. For keys [10,20,30,40], a range 20–35 benefits from an ordered path and neighboring leaves. Index choice depends on predicates, ordering, maintenance cost, and engine support. “An index is O(log n)” hides page I/O and result-size work.

    10.1.4 · LSM trees and write amplification

    An LSM-based engine buffers writes, flushes sorted runs, and compacts them into a searchable organization. Sequential ingestion can help write-heavy workloads, while reads may consult several structures and compaction rewrites data. Write amplification counts physical bytes written relative to logical changes; it depends on layout and workload. Compaction consumes bandwidth and can cause stalls, so provision and observe it. A write-optimized name does not mean unlimited writes or free reads; compare tail latency under sustained ingestion.

    10.1.5 · Query planning and EXPLAIN

    A query planner selects a physical plan from logical operations using statistics and cost estimates. EXPLAIN shows a proposed plan; execution analysis can reveal actual rows and time but may execute side effects depending on the command and engine. A join estimated at ten rows but producing a million can choose an unsuitable strategy. Inspect cardinality estimates, filters, scan types, sorts, and buffers. Update statistics or rewrite the query before blindly adding hardware or indexes.

    10.1.6 · Index selection and query optimization

    An index speeds selected access paths while consuming space and write work. A composite index on (tenant_id,created_at,id) can support a tenant-scoped time-ordered page when the predicates and ordering fit. Unused or redundant indexes slow writes without helping reads. Covering an operation can avoid extra fetches in some engines, but larger indexes reduce cache locality. Test with representative data distribution and parameters; a small uniform fixture may conceal skew and poor selectivity.

    Architecture review · Which invariant becomes harder when a local multi-statement transaction is split across independently owned databases?

    Use claim_seat() against the same store and assert one owner wins while the other receives conflict. Explain which local transaction protects the invariant. Add rollback and crash histories; do not claim a local seat claim makes a remote payment part of the same transaction.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.2

    Commit, logging & versions

    Prerequisites: 10.1 · Pages, indexes & query plans4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two users attempt to purchase the last available ticket. Demonstrate the lost-update race, show why naive reads fail, and implement valid alternatives using transactions and concurrency control.

    This chapter examines commit, logging & versions through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    10.2.1 · ACID properties

    ACID separates atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. Atomicity prevents partial transaction outcomes; consistency means the transaction preserves declared invariants when the application and constraints are correct; isolation governs concurrent observations; durability protects committed state under configuration and failure assumptions. The C is not a promise that all business rules are automatically inferred. A transaction that atomically transfers the wrong amount can satisfy engine mechanics while violating the intended business rule.

    10.2.2 · Transaction commit and rollback

    Commit establishes a transaction's accepted outcome according to the engine's protocol; rollback abandons its uncommitted work. Do not send a business success before commit completes if success requires persistence. Commit can fail or leave the client uncertain after a connection loss. Retrying the transaction may duplicate an external effect unless identity and coordination are explicit. Keep remote provider calls outside long-held local transactions where possible, and reconcile their results rather than pretend rollback reverses a remote charge.

    10.2.3 · Write-ahead logging

    Write-ahead logging records recovery information before the corresponding dirty data pages are considered safely persisted. Recovery can use durable log records to reconstruct committed work even when data pages lag. Checkpointing limits recovery effort; it is not the same as a backup. Acknowledgment behavior depends on sync and replication configuration. Log durability alone cannot protect against loss of the only device containing both log and data, or an application committing logically wrong changes.

    10.2.4 · MVCC

    MVCC maintains versions so readers can observe a defined snapshot while writers create new versions. Visibility depends on transaction rules, not simply the newest timestamp. A long-running reader can retain old versions and delay cleanup. Snapshot reads do not inherently prevent write skew: two transactions may read the same invariant and update different rows. Understand the engine's isolation level and conflict detection rather than treating “uses MVCC” as synonymous with serializable execution.

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.3

    Races, anomalies & isolation

    Prerequisites: 10.2 · Commit, logging & versions5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two users attempt to purchase the last available ticket. Demonstrate the lost-update race, show why naive reads fail, and implement valid alternatives using transactions and concurrency control.

    This chapter examines races, anomalies & isolation through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    10.3.1 · Locking and optimistic concurrency control

    Pessimistic locking coordinates access before conflicting work; optimistic concurrency validates that assumptions still hold before committing. A versioned update such as UPDATE seat SET owner=A,version=8 WHERE id=7 AND version=7 succeeds only if its expected version remains current. Zero affected rows means conflict, not success. Retrying must re-read and reconsider business conditions. Locks can wait or deadlock, while optimistic retries can waste work under contention; choose based on conflict rate and transaction cost.

    10.3.2 · Dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantom reads

    A dirty read observes uncommitted changes; a nonrepeatable read sees a previously read row change; a phantom changes the set matching a predicate. Starting with three open reservations, another transaction inserts a fourth before a repeated predicate query. The anomaly's occurrence depends on isolation and implementation. Do not assume that an isolation level's name implies identical behavior in every database. Define the problematic history and test the selected engine's documented guarantees.

    10.3.3 · Lost updates, write skew, serialization anomalies

    Lost updates overwrite another writer's result; write skew violates a multi-row invariant after transactions update different rows; serialization anomalies are histories without an equivalent serial ordering. If two doctors each see the other on call and both mark themselves off, a snapshot can preserve each read yet violate “at least one on call.” Fix the invariant with appropriate serialization, locking, or a redesigned shared conflict point. Protecting only each individual row is insufficient.

    10.3.4 · Isolation levels and implementation differences

    Isolation levels specify allowed concurrency behavior, but engines implement them differently. PostgreSQL 18 Read Committed uses statement-level snapshots for ordinary reads; its Repeatable Read provides a transaction snapshot yet can permit serialization anomalies; Serializable adds conflict handling that can abort transactions. Other engines and statement forms differ. Applications must handle retryable failures by restarting the whole affected transaction with bounded attempts. Do not retry only the last statement while retaining assumptions from an invalidated snapshot.

    10.3.5 · Serializable execution and serializability

    Serializable means the committed effect is equivalent to some serial transaction order, not necessarily wall-clock order. Linearizability is a distinct real-time single-operation property; strict serializability combines a transactional serial order with real-time constraints. A transaction may need retry after serialization failure. Keep external side effects out of blindly replayed transaction bodies or protect them with stable identity. Serialization makes concurrency reasoning stronger but does not validate incorrect business logic or solve every availability requirement.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.4

    Pools, recovery & ticket correctness

    Prerequisites: 10.3 · Races, anomalies & isolation4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two users attempt to purchase the last available ticket. Demonstrate the lost-update race, show why naive reads fail, and implement valid alternatives using transactions and concurrency control.

    This chapter examines pools, recovery & ticket correctness through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    10.4.1 · Database connection pooling

    A database pool caps active connections and queues acquisition. A larger pool can increase contention and memory rather than throughput. Measure connection hold time, lock waits, idle-in-transaction sessions, and queue age. In an illustrative pool of ten connections with 100 ms mean hold time, the ideal fully busy bound is 100 operations/s before other limits. If callers hold connections while waiting on external HTTP calls, shorten the ownership scope instead of only increasing the pool.

    10.4.2 · Transactions across multiple operations

    A business operation spanning several statements needs one deliberate atomic boundary if its invariant requires all-or-nothing changes. Reserving inventory and recording a local reservation should commit together. An ORM save call is not proof that every related action shares the transaction. Across separate stores or external services, use an explicit distributed protocol or workflow with reconciliation. Transaction scope should be as small as possible while preserving the invariant, and must not leak through lazy results after disposal.

    10.4.3 · Backup, recovery, and durability

    Backups provide recoverable historical state; replication keeps live copies and can replicate mistakes. Test restores into a usable environment and verify application invariants, credentials, schema versions, and recovery time. A backup job reporting success does not prove that its archive is complete or decryptable. Specify point-in-time recovery requirements and how logs are retained. Durability is conditional on acknowledged persistence and independent failure protection, not established by merely owning a backup file.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · conditional seat claim

    from mechanisms import open_demo_store, claim_seat
db = open_demo_store()
db.execute("INSERT INTO seats VALUES (1,NULL)")
db.commit()
assert claim_seat(db, 1, "A")
assert not claim_seat(db, 1, "B")
db.close()

    The conditional update owns the local invariant. The verification suite also uses two connections to one store. External payment and expiry must preserve reservation identity and need their own workflow contract.

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.1

    Locality and cache placement

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A popular product page receives enormous traffic. Introduce caching gradually and examine stale prices, thundering herds, inventory correctness, and failure behavior.

    This chapter examines locality and cache placement through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    11.1.1 · Why caching works

    Caching works when requests reuse data or nearby data often enough to avoid more expensive work. A product description read thousands of times between edits is a candidate; a unique one-use computation may not be. Compare hit latency, miss cost, maintenance, and correctness. With assumed 1 ms hits, 50 ms misses, and 90% hits, the simple weighted service-time average is 5.9 ms, excluding queues and other work. A hit ratio alone does not describe tail latency or cost.

    11.1.2 · Cache locality and the working set

    Temporal locality is reuse over time; spatial locality is reuse of nearby data. The working set is the data actively needed over a relevant interval. A cache too small for that set may churn even if total historical data is enormous. Scan traffic can evict useful entries under some policies. Measure bytes, object sizes, skew, and admission behavior, not only key count. Caching every object eagerly can waste memory on cold data while crowding out hot content.

    11.1.3 · In-process vs distributed caches

    An in-process cache is fast and simple but creates independent copies per application instance. A distributed cache shares a network-accessible state layer, adding serialization, connection, and availability costs. If two app instances cache price 10 and 12, reads differ until policy resolves freshness. Do not place an invariant such as inventory allocation solely in an ordinary stale cache. Choose the location by reuse, memory duplication, required coordination, and failure behavior.

    11.1.4 · Browser, CDN, application, and database caches

    Browser, CDN, application, and database caches sit at different ownership and trust boundaries. A personalized response cached at a public edge without the right key can leak data. A database buffer cache stores pages, while an application cache stores computed representations; invalidating one does not invalidate the other. Draw every copy and define freshness at each layer. Diagnosing a stale response requires knowing which layer answered and which version it held.

    Architecture review · When would a product choose lower availability rather than serve a stale cached value?

    At capacity three, A,B,C,A,D evicts B under ideal LRU. Then pause a reader holding version one, commit version two and invalidate, and resume the stale population. Version checks or another justified protocol must prevent an invalid freshness claim; a short TTL only changes exposure.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Carry forward: Browser representation · Shared edge representation · Application object copy · Database page and committed version.

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.2

    Copies, freshness & eviction

    Prerequisites: 11.1 · Locality and cache placement4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A popular product page receives enormous traffic. Introduce caching gradually and examine stale prices, thundering herds, inventory correctness, and failure behavior.

    This chapter examines copies, freshness & eviction through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    11.2.1 · Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind

    Cache-aside loads after a miss; read-through delegates loading to the cache interface; write-through updates a backing store in the write path; write-behind defers backing persistence. Name the actual ordering and failure semantics because implementations vary. In write-behind, acknowledging only a volatile cache can lose accepted changes. Cache-aside still has races: a delayed reader can populate an old value after a newer write invalidated the key. Use versioning or stronger coordination when freshness requires it.

    11.2.2 · TTL and cache expiration

    A TTL bounds intended residence after insertion, not necessarily the age of the underlying fact when inserted. A cached value already five minutes old with a one-minute TTL can remain six minutes behind its source. Expiration is distinct from eviction, and clients may retain their own copies. Use jitter to avoid synchronized expirations. Choose TTL from tolerated staleness and refresh behavior; correctness-critical actions should validate authoritative state rather than trust a display cache.

    11.2.3 · Cache consistency and invalidation

    Invalidation coordinates derived copies with authoritative changes. Delete-after-write is common but cannot by itself prevent every stale repopulation race. Versioned cache entries, conditional population, or source-version checks can strengthen semantics. Events for invalidation can lag or repeat, so observe version and propagation time. For prices, stale display may be acceptable while checkout revalidates the current price; for inventory, accepting stale availability as authority can oversell. Match the cache contract to the operation's invariant.

    11.2.4 · Eviction: LRU, LFU, FIFO, and alternatives

    LRU favors recent access; LFU favors frequent access; FIFO evicts insertion order. Their precise implementations may be approximate. For capacity three and accesses A,B,C,A,D, ideal LRU evicts B; FIFO evicts A; a frequency-based policy also needs tie-breaking. Compare policies with representative traffic and object sizes. A clever eviction algorithm cannot fix a working set vastly beyond memory or a cache that stores low-value objects indiscriminately. Admission and eviction are separate choices.

    Architecture review · When would a product choose lower availability rather than serve a stale cached value?

    At capacity three, A,B,C,A,D evicts B under ideal LRU. Then pause a reader holding version one, commit version two and invalidate, and resume the stale population. Version checks or another justified protocol must prevent an invalid freshness claim; a short TTL only changes exposure.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    A clever eviction algorithm cannot fix a working set vastly beyond memory or a cache that stores low-value objects indiscriminately.

    Carry forward: Capacity: 3 entries · Access A, B, C, A · Insert D · LRU removes B; FIFO removes A.

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.3

    Hot keys, stampedes & negative results

    Prerequisites: 11.2 · Copies, freshness & eviction5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A popular product page receives enormous traffic. Introduce caching gradually and examine stale prices, thundering herds, inventory correctness, and failure behavior.

    This chapter examines hot keys, stampedes & negative results through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    11.3.1 · Hot keys

    A hot key concentrates traffic on one shard or owner. More cache nodes do not distribute a single key automatically. Options include local read copies, replication where supported, request coalescing, or deliberate partitioning of commutative aggregates. Each affects freshness or aggregation cost. For a stock count, blindly splitting into independent counters can violate allocation correctness. First identify whether the pressure is read bandwidth, write serialization, object size, or repeated recomputation.

    11.3.2 · Cache stampedes, penetration, and avalanche

    A stampede occurs when many misses trigger duplicate expensive work. Penetration repeatedly requests absent keys; an avalanche is a broad synchronized loss or expiry of cached entries. Use single-flight loading, bounded refresh workers, negative caching, TTL jitter, and origin admission limits as appropriate. Locks used for refresh also need expiration and failure handling. A cache outage should not let every application instance independently overwhelm the database while attempting to reconstruct the entire working set.

    11.3.3 · Negative caching

    Negative caching stores an absence or error under a narrow policy. Caching “product not found” for a short interval can protect against repeated nonexistent lookups. Do not cache a temporary database failure as permanent absence, and do not let one tenant's authorization failure poison another tenant's key. A newly created product may remain hidden until negative-entry expiry or invalidation. Use separate error types, short appropriate lifetimes, and correctly scoped keys.

    11.3.4 · Stale-while-revalidate

    Stale-while-revalidate serves an allowed stale value while one refresh updates it. This trades freshness for latency and origin protection; it is not suitable for every operation. A cached description can be stale, while payment authorization cannot be inferred from an old response. Define fresh, stale-allowed, and unusable age limits. If refresh repeatedly fails, do not extend stale serving forever unless that is an explicit degradation contract visible to users and operators.

    11.3.5 · Cache warming and prefetching

    Warming preloads likely useful entries; prefetching predicts near-future requests. Both consume bandwidth and may evict more valuable content. Warm a measured working set gradually after deployment rather than issuing a full-database scan from every new instance. Track whether prefetched entries are actually used and cancel obsolete work. A cold-start problem may be better addressed through staggered rollout, shared cache layers, or request admission than an increasingly elaborate prediction system.

    Architecture review · When would a product choose lower availability rather than serve a stale cached value?

    At capacity three, A,B,C,A,D evicts B under ideal LRU. Then pause a reader holding version one, commit version two and invalidate, and resume the stale population. Version checks or another justified protocol must prevent an invalid freshness claim; a short TTL only changes exposure.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.4

    Edges, partitions & the price of a cache

    Prerequisites: 11.3 · Hot keys, stampedes & negative results4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A popular product page receives enormous traffic. Introduce caching gradually and examine stale prices, thundering herds, inventory correctness, and failure behavior.

    This chapter examines edges, partitions & the price of a cache through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    11.4.1 · Redis-like data structures

    Redis-like structures include strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams, each with different operations and cost models. A sorted set can track a time-ordered window; a set can deduplicate identifiers within a lifecycle. Atomicity of one command is not automatically atomicity of a multi-command workflow. Server-side scripts or transactions may provide the needed local boundary, but durability, replication, cluster key placement, and expiry still matter. Do not assume every structure is a durable queue by default.

    11.4.2 · CDN architecture and origin shielding

    An edge cache serves representations near clients, while an origin shield can consolidate misses before the origin. Signed URLs and cache keys need policy: query parameters, headers, tenant identity, and content versions can change what is safe to share. A purge request propagates under the provider's contract and may not invalidate every client-held copy. Use immutable versioned asset URLs when practical. Delivery improves bandwidth and latency for suitable content but does not authorize serving private data globally.

    11.4.3 · Cache partitioning and replication

    Partitioning distributes keys; replication creates copies for resilience or reads under a protocol. A cache may lose or evict entries during failover, and replicas may lag. The application must decide whether to fall back, serve allowed stale data, or reject. Consistent hashing reduces some remapping during membership changes but cannot prevent hot-key skew. Keep cache and authoritative-store failure domains and recovery capacity explicit; rebuilding after a cluster event can be the real peak workload.

    11.4.4 · When caching is harmful

    Caching is harmful when maintenance and correctness cost exceed saved work. A low-reuse result cache may consume memory and serialization time without many hits. A cache with missing authorization scope can leak data; one that masks a slow database during normal operation can hide an origin capacity deficit until outage. Test the system with the cache empty or unavailable. Prefer query/index improvements or simpler data access when they address the bottleneck with fewer state copies.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · ideal LRU

    from mechanisms import LRU
cache = LRU(3)
for key in "ABC": cache.put(key, key)
cache.get("A")
assert cache.put("D", "D") == ("B", "B")

    The ideal LRU example is deterministic. Production engines can approximate policy, include byte limits, and treat expiration separately. Eviction behavior alone says nothing about source freshness or safe cache-aside population.

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.1

    Scale compute & route requests

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Caching and Content Delivery6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Scale a URL shortener from 100 requests per second to 100,000. Introduce new components only when justified by a demonstrated bottleneck.

    This chapter examines scale compute & route requests through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    12.1.1 · Vertical vs horizontal scaling

    Vertical scaling increases resources of one node; horizontal scaling adds nodes. Neither guarantees proportional throughput. A larger database host may buy time without distributed data management, while extra stateless application instances can distribute independent compute. Shared locks, disks, or downstream services can remain limiting. Compare failure impact, scaling delay, cost, and operational complexity. Choose the smallest change supported by profiling, then rerun the workload because the limiting resource can move.

    12.1.2 · Stateless vs stateful services

    A stateless service retains no required per-client conversational state locally between requests; it still operates on state elsewhere. This makes instance replacement and traffic distribution easier. A server-local session or uncommitted job can prevent transparent failover. Move required state to an appropriate owner, or make affinity and recovery explicit. Sending every request to any instance is safe only if identity, state access, configuration, and side-effect handling are compatible across those instances.

    12.1.3 · Load distribution algorithms

    Round-robin spreads selections, least-connections approximates active load, weighted policies reflect capacity, and hashing can preserve affinity. Their effectiveness depends on request cost and connection behavior. One expensive request can occupy a backend much longer than many cheap ones. Observe queueing and per-instance saturation, not only request counts. Client-side or server-side balancing also affects discovery, retries, and failure detection. A distribution algorithm cannot create capacity at a saturated shared database.

    12.1.4 · Health checks and failover

    Health checks approximate readiness, not omniscient correctness. Liveness asks whether a process should be restarted; readiness asks whether it should receive traffic under the chosen policy. A check that requires every downstream service can remove all instances during a shared dependency outage and worsen recovery. Use meaningful local signals, bounded checks, and deliberate degradation policy. Failover also requires state and connection behavior that support the switch; routing alone does not recover uncommitted work.

    12.1.5 · Sticky sessions

    Sticky sessions keep a client associated with an instance and can support local state or reduce cache misses. They also create uneven load and complicate failover. A user's connection may outlive the instance, so required state needs recovery or an explicit reconnection protocol. Prefer external session ownership for simple replaceable web instances when feasible. Affinity is an optimization or a deliberate constraint, not a substitute for deciding where authoritative state lives.

    12.1.6 · Autoscaling metrics

    Autoscaling reacts to a measured signal, with delay and limits. CPU may suit compute-heavy workers, queue age may better represent background latency, and connection saturation may expose an I/O bottleneck. Scaling on request count alone assumes similar cost per request. Use stabilization and maximums to avoid oscillation or runaway spend. Provision startup headroom and admission control so a sudden spike does not exhaust the system before new capacity becomes ready.

    Architecture review · Can a single globally hot invariant be scaled merely by adding more partitions? Explain the constraint.

    For many deterministic keys, a key either keeps its old owner or moves to the new owner in this model. That property does not guarantee balanced request traffic. Make one key extremely popular and show why adding cold owners cannot split that single-key pressure without a new serving strategy.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Use stabilization and maximums to avoid oscillation or runaway spend.

    Carry forward: Metric crosses threshold · Controller requests capacity · Instances start and warm · Admission limits protect the delay.

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.2

    Replicate and partition data

    Prerequisites: 12.1 · Scale compute & route requests6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Scale a URL shortener from 100 requests per second to 100,000. Introduce new components only when justified by a demonstrated bottleneck.

    This chapter examines replicate and partition data through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    12.2.1 · Replication

    Replication maintains copies under an acknowledgment and reconciliation protocol. It can improve availability or read distribution, but may introduce lag, conflict, and acknowledged-write-loss risks depending on configuration. Async replication can acknowledge before a replica has the write; sync replication can increase latency or block during failure. State which replicas are required for acknowledgment and which failures promotion tolerates. A second copy is not a proof of durability without independent failure domains and recovery rules.

    12.2.2 · Partitioning and sharding

    Partitioning divides a dataset; sharding commonly distributes those partitions across separate storage owners. Choose a key that supports important queries and distributes work. Sharding by tenant can isolate some traffic but leave one large tenant hot. Cross-shard joins, uniqueness, transactions, and migrations become more complex. Keep a routing model and relocation procedure. Add partitioning when a measured storage or write bottleneck justifies it, rather than assuming every large user count requires it.

    12.2.3 · Range partitioning vs hash partitioning

    Range partitioning preserves ordered locality and can make time-based retention efficient, but a newest range may receive most writes. Hash partitioning spreads keys more evenly while making ordered scans and range locality harder. Neither avoids skew if one key dominates. For event ingestion, partitioning only by current day concentrates all writers; combining a time bucket with a spread dimension can help at the cost of multi-partition reads. Define the resulting query fan-out.

    12.2.4 · Consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing

    Consistent hashing places keys and owners in a mapping that changes only part of the assignment when membership changes; virtual nodes can improve distribution. Rendezvous hashing scores each key-owner pair and chooses the highest eligible score, offering a different implementation of stable assignment. Neither guarantees equal traffic because request popularity is not uniform. Membership agreement, migration, replication, and hot-key handling remain required. Avoid changing hash functions without a plan for old data and client routing.

    12.2.5 · Rebalancing

    Rebalancing moves data or ownership while serving traffic. A robust move copies a snapshot, captures concurrent changes, validates catch-up, and changes routing under an ownership epoch or equivalent protocol. Readers and writers must not disagree indefinitely about the owner. Throttle movement so it does not consume all production I/O. Keep a rollback and reconciliation path; deleting the old copy before the new owner is authoritative can turn a routine capacity change into data loss.

    12.2.6 · Hot partitions and skew

    Hot partitions arise from uneven key popularity, data size, or write concentration. A heatmap of requests and bytes per partition reveals skew hidden by fleet averages. Splitting a range may help if traffic divides; a single hot entity may need read copies, batching, or a redesigned invariant owner. Randomizing writes can distribute append pressure but makes reads aggregate more partitions. Match the fix to the actual pressure rather than repeatedly adding cold capacity.

    Architecture review · Can a single globally hot invariant be scaled merely by adding more partitions? Explain the constraint.

    For many deterministic keys, a key either keeps its old owner or moves to the new owner in this model. That property does not guarantee balanced request traffic. Make one key extremely popular and show why adding cold owners cannot split that single-key pressure without a new serving strategy.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Randomizing writes can distribute append pressure but makes reads aggregate more partitions.

    Carry forward: Fleet average appears healthy · One partition receives 70% of writes · Its queue determines tail latency · Split or redesign the specific hot path.

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.3

    Lag, proxies & saturated pools

    Prerequisites: 12.2 · Replicate and partition data5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Scale a URL shortener from 100 requests per second to 100,000. Introduce new components only when justified by a demonstrated bottleneck.

    This chapter examines lag, proxies & saturated pools through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    12.3.1 · Read replicas and read/write splitting

    Read replicas can distribute suitable reads while the primary retains writes. A read immediately after an update can observe stale data if routed to a lagging replica. Route critical reads to a sufficiently current owner, use session position tracking where supported, or accept an explicit freshness contract. Read/write splitting must classify operations by required semantics, not only by SQL verb: a SELECT may participate in a consistency-critical transaction or require a lock.

    12.3.2 · Replication lag

    Replication lag is the distance between source and replica state, measured by time, positions, or application version. A small average lag can hide a replica stalled for a particular workload. Expose source progress and replica apply progress, and distinguish transport lag from apply lag. Users may need read-your-writes even when global reads tolerate eventual freshness. Failover decisions must account for lag and acknowledged-write policy; the fastest promotion is not necessarily the safest promotion.

    12.3.3 · Database proxying

    A database proxy can pool, route, or multiplex connections according to implementation. It does not remove database transaction limits and can change session-state assumptions. A client using session variables, temporary tables, or long transactions may not be safe under arbitrary multiplexing. Document where authentication, routing, and failover decisions happen. The proxy itself needs capacity and failure handling; placing it in a diagram does not eliminate connection saturation or guarantee transparent retries.

    12.3.4 · Connection pool saturation

    When a pool is full, waiting callers accumulate outside the database as well as inside it. More application replicas can multiply total database connections beyond the safe limit. Bound the aggregate across instances, reserve recovery capacity, and include acquisition time in deadlines. A query waiting on a lock may hold its connection while doing no CPU work. Fix hold time, contention, and admission before expanding every pool and increasing the pressure that caused the queue.

    12.3.5 · Bottleneck identification

    Bottleneck diagnosis follows the critical path and resource saturation. Compare offered load, good completions, queues, CPU, memory, disk, network, connection waits, and lock contention. If a single database query dominates, caching or indexing may help more than extra web instances; if CPU is saturated with independent work, compute scaling may help. Change one material variable and measure again. A component's high utilization is a clue, not proof that it limits the business outcome.

    Architecture review · Can a single globally hot invariant be scaled merely by adding more partitions? Explain the constraint.

    For many deterministic keys, a key either keeps its old owner or moves to the new owner in this model. That property does not guarantee balanced request traffic. Make one key extremely popular and show why adding cold owners cannot split that single-key pressure without a new serving strategy.
