    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.4

    Regions, write paths & scale economics

    Prerequisites: 12.3 · Lag, proxies & saturated pools5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Scale a URL shortener from 100 requests per second to 100,000. Introduce new components only when justified by a demonstrated bottleneck.

    This chapter examines regions, write paths & scale economics through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    12.4.1 · Queueing and overload

    A queue absorbs temporary mismatch, not sustained overload. If arrivals exceed completion, the queue grows until latency, memory, or a limit fails. Bound queue size and age, reject or shed excess work, and prioritize essential operations. Waiting longer can make a request useless while still consuming resources. With a two-second deadline, a ten-second backlog should not be silently accepted as if work were on time. Return an explicit overload outcome and avoid automatic retry storms.

    12.4.2 · Single points of failure

    A single point of failure can be a machine, database, credentials service, router, operator action, or shared dependency. Count independent failure domains rather than only process replicas. Two application containers on one host do not survive that host's loss. Redundancy also needs failover, capacity, detection, and state correctness. Inspect control-plane dependencies during recovery: the data path may be redundant while a missing configuration service prevents every replacement instance from starting.

    12.4.3 · Multi-region strategies

    Multi-region designs trade latency, data placement, conflict, cost, and failure behavior. Active-passive can simplify write ownership but requires tested promotion and recovery targets. Active-active may improve locality or continuity but needs a precise conflict or coordination model. Cross-region acknowledgment adds propagation delay; asynchronous copies can lose recent acknowledged writes on failover. Start with business requirements for locality, tolerated interruption, and data loss, then choose write authority and read contracts per operation.

    12.4.4 · Scaling writes vs scaling reads

    Read scaling often replicates or caches immutable or sufficiently stale-tolerant data. Write scaling must distribute, batch, or reduce ownership work while preserving invariants. A globally unique sequential allocator or one hot account can remain serialized across many shards. Reduce unnecessary indexes or coordination before distributing more components. Aggregate counters may allow commutative updates, while seat allocation needs exclusive ownership. Different business operations can legitimately use different scaling and consistency strategies.

    12.4.5 · Scale-out economics

    Scale-out economics includes duplicate baseline capacity, coordination, networking, telemetry, cache warmup, and operational work. Ten small nodes are not automatically cheaper or faster than one larger node. Compare equal service objectives and failure headroom under the same workload; include the capacity required during a node or zone loss. Managed systems can trade provider charges against staffing and recovery work. Use cost per successful business outcome and investigate bottlenecks before purchasing capacity that cannot help.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · stable rendezvous mapping

    from mechanisms import rendezvous
for key in range(1000):
    old = rendezvous(key, ["A","B","C"])
    new = rendezvous(key, ["A","B","C","D"])
    assert old == new or new == "D"

    Adding an owner moves only keys now won by that owner in this model. It does not transfer data, synchronize membership, or distribute one hot key. Those protocols and workload effects remain explicit design work.

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.1

    Upload bytes without losing identity

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a document-processing system accepting millions of files, tracking processing state, extracting metadata, maintaining provenance, and exposing searchable results.

    This chapter examines upload bytes without losing identity through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    13.1.1 · Binary/object storage

    Store large binary content separately from mutable processing metadata when their access and lifecycle needs differ. An object has a stable identity, content version or checksum, size, and ownership metadata; a job record references it. A database row pointing at a missing or incomplete object is a broken workflow even if both services individually succeed. Use explicit upload states and cleanup for abandoned bytes. Treat object-store-specific consistency and durability claims as implementation contracts to verify, not category-wide assumptions.

    13.1.2 · Large-file upload architecture

    A large-file architecture can issue a scoped upload authorization so the client streams directly to storage, while the application owns metadata and authorization. This avoids proxying all bytes through web workers, but the client may never complete the upload. Validate ownership, quotas, content size, and completion evidence before making a file available for processing. Expire abandoned intents and reconcile unreferenced objects. A signed upload URL is a time-bounded capability that must not grant arbitrary bucket access.

    13.1.3 · Multipart and resumable uploads

    Multipart upload splits a file into identifiable parts with explicit completion. Resumability tracks confirmed offsets or parts so a client can retry without restarting all bytes. Duplicate part submission and changed source content need defined behavior. Verify the completed object rather than assuming every acknowledged part implies a correct final file. Multipart identifiers and checksums can be provider-specific; a convenient entity tag is not universally a content hash. Clean up incomplete sessions to prevent silent storage growth.

    13.1.4 · Checksums and content addressing

    A checksum detects accidental corruption under its algorithm's properties; a cryptographic digest can identify content with collision assumptions and appropriate verification. Content addressing uses a digest-derived identity, enabling deduplication or immutable references. It does not authorize access or prove the content is safe. Scope deduplication carefully across tenants to avoid information leakage, and verify downloaded bytes when integrity matters. A hash of a client-provided claim is not a checksum of the bytes actually stored.

    13.1.5 · Metadata vs binary data

    Binary bytes and metadata have different update patterns. Keep file identity and immutable byte versions distinct from classification status, user annotations, and processing attempts. An extractor should record exactly which content and model version produced an output. Mutating a file in place under the same identifier can make old results impossible to explain. If the input changes, create a new version and schedule appropriate reprocessing while retaining or deleting historical artifacts according to policy.

    Architecture review · How would you reproduce a disputed extracted field after both the source and model have new versions?

    Use Workflow to reject stale epochs and wrong input versions. Retain exact source and transform versions. Build a new index generation, account for concurrent changes and deletions, validate, and switch a serving pointer. Matching record counts alone is not sufficient evidence of correct versions or authorization.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.2

    Build and rebuild a search index

    Prerequisites: 13.1 · Upload bytes without losing identity4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a document-processing system accepting millions of files, tracking processing state, extracting metadata, maintaining provenance, and exposing searchable results.

    This chapter examines build and rebuild a search index through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    13.2.1 · Search engines and inverted indexes

    An inverted index maps a term to postings describing documents or positions containing it. For documents D1='blue car' and D2='blue bike', blue maps to D1,D2 while car maps only to D1. Analysis choices such as tokenization and normalization affect matching. Search updates need document identity and version to prevent an old extraction from replacing a newer one. Keep source records rebuildable; the index is a derived serving structure with its own freshness and permission obligations.

    13.2.2 · Indexing pipelines

    An indexing pipeline transforms authoritative content into searchable representations. Separate extraction, validation, enrichment, indexing, and publication states so a partial failure is diagnosable. Retry a stage using stable input and output identities; avoid creating duplicate documents on every retry. Poison files need bounded attempts and a review path. Check that index permissions derive from current ownership rather than stale public flags embedded in an old output. Completion should refer to a precise index version and source version.

    13.2.3 · Search ingestion and reindexing

    Reindexing builds a new representation while preserving serving behavior. Take a snapshot or defined source position, process its records, catch up subsequent changes, validate, and switch a serving alias or routing epoch. Do not overwrite the only working index before the new one is verified. Deletions and updates during the build need replay or reconciliation. Rollback must preserve schema compatibility and any new writes; counting indexed documents alone cannot establish that the right versions or permissions were indexed.

    Architecture review · How would you reproduce a disputed extracted field after both the source and model have new versions?

    Use Workflow to reject stale epochs and wrong input versions. Retain exact source and transform versions. Build a new index generation, account for concurrent changes and deletions, validate, and switch a serving pointer. Matching record counts alone is not sufficient evidence of correct versions or authorization.

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.3

    Move data through batch and streams

    Prerequisites: 13.2 · Build and rebuild a search index5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a document-processing system accepting millions of files, tracking processing state, extracting metadata, maintaining provenance, and exposing searchable results.

    This chapter examines move data through batch and streams through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    13.3.1 · Batch vs streaming pipelines

    Batch processing operates on bounded sets; stream processing operates on continuing input with explicit progress and state. A nightly export may be simpler when hours of freshness delay are acceptable; fraud signals may require lower-latency updates. Streaming introduces late data, state recovery, partitioning, and checkpoint concerns. Batch can still be expensive and failure-prone. Choose based on freshness and recomputation needs, and specify whether results are provisional or final when late events can change them.

    13.3.2 · ETL vs ELT

    ETL transforms before loading into the target; ELT loads and transforms in the target environment. ETL can minimize sensitive fields before they reach an analytical store; ELT can preserve flexible raw inputs but increases governance and storage obligations. Either can lose lineage or silently change semantics if transformations are undocumented. Version transformations, validate schemas, and define ownership of raw and derived datasets. The acronym does not determine quality, privacy, or repeatability.

    13.3.3 · Change Data Capture (CDC)

    Change Data Capture emits committed changes from a source through a supported mechanism such as a transaction log. It can keep search or analytics current without polling entire tables. A snapshot plus a change stream needs a consistent handoff position so writes are neither missed nor applied incorrectly. Events can repeat, and schema changes affect decoding. Preserve source identity and ordering metadata, deduplicate, and monitor lag. CDC does not automatically make the destination transactionally consistent with the source for every query.

    13.3.4 · Data lakes and warehouses

    A data lake stores flexible datasets, often in object storage; a warehouse provides curated analytical structures and serving capabilities. Boundaries vary by product. Raw retention can help replay but also accumulates privacy, quality, and discovery problems. A lake without schema, ownership, and lineage becomes difficult to trust. Model immutable inputs, curated outputs, catalog metadata, access policies, and lifecycle separately. Choose formats and partitioning for the queries and recovery operations that actually need to run.

    13.3.5 · Stream processing fundamentals

    Stream processing maintains results over ongoing events using windows, keys, and state. Event time describes when a source event occurred; processing time describes when it was handled. Watermarks estimate progress under assumptions about late arrivals; they are not proof that no earlier event can ever arrive. Define allowed lateness, correction behavior, checkpoint ownership, and effect boundaries. A windowed count can be updated after a late event, so consumers need to understand whether it is provisional or final.

    Architecture review · How would you reproduce a disputed extracted field after both the source and model have new versions?

    Use Workflow to reject stale epochs and wrong input versions. Retain exact source and transform versions. Build a new index generation, account for concurrent changes and deletions, validate, and switch a serving pointer. Matching record counts alone is not sufficient evidence of correct versions or authorization.

    PART 3 / UNIT 13 / CHAPTER 13.4

    Quality, provenance & replay

    Prerequisites: 13.3 · Move data through batch and streams4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design a document-processing system accepting millions of files, tracking processing state, extracting metadata, maintaining provenance, and exposing searchable results.

    This chapter examines quality, provenance & replay through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    13.4.1 · Data provenance and lineage

    Provenance records where an artifact came from; lineage connects transformations between artifacts. An extracted amount should link to file version, page or region, extractor version, parameters, and review decisions. This supports debugging and correction without claiming the extraction is always right. Store stable references, not only a text explanation that cannot be checked. Privacy and retention apply to provenance too; an audit trail containing raw personal data can outlive the source if lifecycle policies are incomplete.

    13.4.2 · Data quality, schema validation, and replay

    Data quality checks validate shape, ranges, identity, relationships, and completeness against explicit contracts. Schema-valid records can still be semantically wrong: a currency field may be present but incompatible with the amount units. Quarantine invalid inputs with reasons and preserve enough evidence for repair. Replay must be versioned and deduplicated so fixing a transformation does not double side effects. Compare counts, versions, and business invariants at source and sink rather than trusting an empty error queue.

    13.4.3 · Lifecycle policies and retention

    Lifecycle policies should follow every copy: raw files, extracted text, thumbnails, indexes, logs, and backups. A retention timer on the original PDF alone leaves derived personal data behind. Use deletion workflows with durable progress and reconciliation; maintain narrowly scoped tombstones where required to prevent replay resurrection. Large object collections need efficient listing or ownership indexes for deletion. Test recovery from old snapshots against deletion history so a restore does not silently reverse required privacy actions.

    13.4.4 · Designing data-intensive applications

    A data-intensive design is a network of state transformations, not a collection of product logos. For every edge, define source authority, version, ordering, retry identity, validation, ownership, and recovery. Keep immutable source versions so derived structures can be rebuilt, but do not retain everything indefinitely without purpose. End-to-end reliability comes from coordinating those contracts and observing progress across the pipeline. A scalable queue cannot compensate for an extractor that loses provenance or an index that serves unauthorized copies.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · source and attempt fencing

    from mechanisms import Workflow
run = Workflow("file-version-2", epoch=8)
assert not run.complete(7, "file-version-2", "old")
assert not run.complete(8, "file-version-1", "wrong-input")
assert run.complete(8, "file-version-2", "current")

    The miniature checks local identity and epoch. Persisting it safely requires an atomic storage transition and output validation. Provenance must also record transformation versions and relevant source regions, not just an artifact name.

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.1

    Partial failure & the meaning of time

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control7 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A social application writes a new post in one region while a friend reads it from another. Examine different consistency contracts and their user-visible effects.

    This chapter examines partial failure & the meaning of time through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    14.1.1 · What makes a distributed system difficult?

    Distribution removes the ability to observe one coherent machine state. A request may succeed on one node while another is unreachable, and a caller may not know whether a timed-out write committed. Designing a distributed system means specifying allowed histories under those uncertainties. Begin with one authoritative owner and explicit operations; add replication or coordination to meet a concrete need. Additional nodes create failure combinations as well as capacity, so correctness must be a protocol rather than a diagram of reachable boxes.

    14.1.2 · Partial failures

    A partial failure affects some participants or paths while others keep operating. The payment provider can charge successfully while the order service loses the reply. Rolling back the local order cannot reverse that external event. Track an uncertain state with a stable provider reference and reconcile it. Design compensations only for effects that can actually be compensated, and distinguish an operation not attempted from one attempted with unknown outcome. Treating every exception as a clean failure creates duplicate business effects.

    14.1.3 · Network uncertainty

    A slow network and a failed node can look the same to a participant for a while. Timeouts are practical failure suspicions, not perfect failure detectors. A retry can reach another node after the original is merely delayed. Use deadlines and bounded retries to protect resources, but let the protocol prevent conflicting owners or duplicate effects. Availability decisions must state when the system prefers rejecting work to risking an invariant, rather than assuming every missing heartbeat proves the old owner stopped.

    14.1.4 · Fault models

    A fault model states what kinds of failure a protocol tolerates: crash-stop, crash-recovery, message loss, partitions, or arbitrary Byzantine behavior. A majority algorithm designed for non-malicious crash failures does not automatically tolerate participants lying about their logs. Durability also depends on whether persistent state survives restart and on failure independence. Name these assumptions before counting nodes. Three replicas on one failing device do not provide the same protection as independent durable replicas.

    14.1.5 · Time, clocks, and event ordering

    Wall clocks support timestamps and scheduling but can drift, jump, or be adjusted. A timestamp earlier than another does not necessarily establish causality across machines. Duration measurement should use an appropriate monotonic clock where available. If a reservation expires based on time, define the authoritative clock and tolerated uncertainty. Ordering requirements often need a logical sequence or consensus log rather than trusting client-generated timestamps. Record both source and observed time when their distinction matters for debugging.

    14.1.6 · Physical vs logical clocks

    Physical clocks estimate real time; logical clocks represent ordering constraints. A logical counter can advance without representing seconds, while a physical timestamp can compare unrelated events without proving causal order. Use physical time for user-facing dates and appropriate deadline policies, and logical order for protocol relationships where needed. Combining them requires a precise model. Do not subtract two arbitrary hosts' timestamps and call the result network latency without accounting for clock synchronization error.

    14.1.7 · Lamport clocks and vector clocks

    Lamport clocks advance locally and on receive using max(local,received)+1. If event A happens before B through program or message order, its Lamport value is smaller; the converse need not hold. Vector clocks track per-participant causal progress and can identify concurrent versions under their assumptions, at metadata cost. An example with vectors [1,0] and [0,1] is concurrent. Neither clock by itself resolves a conflict or establishes a global real-time commit order.

    Architecture review · During a partition, which operations could degrade while exclusive allocation must wait or reject?

    lamport_receive(5,9) returns 10; vectors [1,0] and [0,1] are concurrent. For three fixed members, R=2,W=2 intersects. Explain why these calculations do not independently resolve concurrent business updates or prove linearizability. The missing protocol rules are part of the answer.

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.2

    Consistency as a reader-visible contract

    Prerequisites: 14.1 · Partial failure & the meaning of time6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A social application writes a new post in one region while a friend reads it from another. Examine different consistency contracts and their user-visible effects.

    This chapter examines consistency as a reader-visible contract through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    14.2.1 · Consistency models

    A consistency model defines legal observation histories. Ask what a user may read after a write, after switching replicas, and after seeing another user's action. A post body and a feed count can have different needs. Stronger constraints can require coordination or reduce allowed serving behavior during partitions. “Strong” is ambiguous without naming the model, and “eventual” alone omits conflict and freshness details. Write concrete histories and identify which observations are acceptable before selecting a database setting.

    14.2.2 · Strong consistency and eventual consistency

    Strong consistency is often used informally for linearizable behavior, but must be defined in context. Eventual convergence says replicas should agree after updates cease and communication and repair assumptions hold; it does not promise a fixed staleness bound or excuse lost acknowledged writes. A display feed may accept temporary delay while the author's profile reads its own post promptly. Specify per-operation behavior and conflict resolution rather than labeling the whole application with one vague adjective.

    14.2.3 · Linearizability

    Linearizability makes completed operations appear to take effect atomically at points between invocation and response, respecting real-time precedence. If a write of 2 completes before a read starts, the read cannot return the overwritten 1 in a linearizable register. Concurrent operations can admit more than one valid ordering. Implementing the property requires a suitable protocol, not only majority counts or wall-clock timestamps. A timed-out operation may still have taken effect because it lacks a completed response.

    14.2.4 · Serializability vs linearizability

    Serializability concerns equivalence of transactions to a serial execution; linearizability concerns real-time atomic behavior of operations. A serial order need not follow observed wall-clock order unless a stronger contract requires it. Strict serializability combines serial transaction behavior with real-time precedence. These distinctions matter when a system mixes transactions, replica reads, and external messages. A serializable database transaction does not automatically make a payment provider call part of one real-time atomic operation.

    14.2.5 · Sequential and causal consistency

    Sequential consistency preserves each participant's program order in some shared ordering without necessarily honoring real-time order across participants. Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect dependencies while allowing unrelated concurrent events to be observed in different orders. If a reply depends on seeing a post, exposing the reply before its parent violates that causal relationship. Metadata and dependency tracking can enforce it, but an ordinary replication delay setting alone does not establish a causal contract.

    14.2.6 · Read-your-writes and monotonic reads

    Read-your-writes keeps a session from losing visibility of its own completed updates; monotonic reads prevent that session from moving backward in observed progress. They can be implemented through routing affinity, replication-position tracking, or suitable protocols. They are session guarantees, not necessarily global linearizability. A user switching devices needs a policy for carrying session progress. Sticky routing alone can fail after an instance change, so define how the guarantee survives failover or when a read must wait.

    lamport_receive(5,9) returns 10; vectors [1,0] and [0,1] are concurrent. For three fixed members, R=2,W=2 intersects. Explain why these calculations do not independently resolve concurrent business updates or prove linearizability. The missing protocol rules are part of the answer.

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.3

    Partitions, CAP, PACELC & quorums

    Prerequisites: 14.2 · Consistency as a reader-visible contract4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A social application writes a new post in one region while a friend reads it from another. Examine different consistency contracts and their user-visible effects.

    This chapter examines partitions, cap, pacelc & quorums through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    14.3.1 · CAP theorem, with its actual assumptions

    CAP's impossibility applies to a defined distributed read/write model under partitions: its formal atomic consistency and availability cannot both be guaranteed for every allowed execution. It is not a menu where a system permanently picks any two attractive qualities. When replicas cannot communicate, an application may reject some operations to protect invariants or serve bounded weaker behavior for others. State the affected operation, partition assumption, and required property. Normal nonpartitioned latency trade-offs require additional reasoning.

    14.3.2 · PACELC as a useful extension

    PACELC highlights two questions: during a partition, availability versus consistency; otherwise, latency versus consistency under the considered design. It is a useful classification lens, not a universal theorem replacing a protocol specification. Waiting for a geographically distant acknowledgment can increase write latency even when the network is healthy. Different operations can choose different paths. Quantify propagation and coordination costs with explicit assumptions, and avoid assigning a permanent one-letter label to a product without checking its configuration.

    14.3.3 · Quorums and read/write trade-offs

    With fixed N replicas, R+W>N ensures a read set intersects a write set; W>N/2 ensures two write quorums intersect. These are set properties, not a complete proof of linearizability. Version ordering, concurrent writes, durable acknowledgments, membership, and read repair matter. Sloppy quorums or changing membership can invalidate naive assumptions. In N=3,R=2,W=2, a read sees at least one participant in a completed write set, but still needs a correct rule for interpreting returned versions.

    14.3.4 · Split-brain situations

    Split brain means participants act as conflicting authorities. A partitioned old leader may keep running after another is elected. A failure detector cannot directly stop it. Use an ownership protocol and enforce epochs or fencing at the resource that accepts effects. Merely expiring a client-side lock variable is insufficient if an old worker can still write to storage. Test paused workers and delayed messages, not only clean process termination.

    PART 4 / UNIT 14 / CHAPTER 14.4

    Coordination, safety & liveness

    Prerequisites: 14.3 · Partitions, CAP, PACELC & quorums4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A social application writes a new post in one region while a friend reads it from another. Examine different consistency contracts and their user-visible effects.

    This chapter examines coordination, safety & liveness through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    14.4.1 · Distributed coordination

    Coordination establishes shared decisions such as ownership, configuration, or ordered metadata. Use it for invariants that genuinely need agreement, while avoiding a coordination round for independent operations that can safely commute. A coordinator must itself have a failure and recovery protocol; making one service named coordinator does not make it reliable. Bound how clients behave when it is unavailable, and distinguish cached configuration serving from issuing new exclusive ownership.

    14.4.2 · The fallacies of distributed computing

    The fallacies of distributed computing warn against assuming reliable networks, zero latency, infinite bandwidth, static topology, free transport, homogeneous infrastructure, automatic security, or one administrator. Translate each into a concrete design check. A serialized payload crossing a team boundary needs version and authorization policy; a large fan-out needs latency and bandwidth accounting. These warnings are engineering prompts rather than formal guarantees. Use them to discover hidden assumptions in a diagram before an outage discovers them for you.

    14.4.3 · Safety vs liveness

    Safety excludes bad outcomes; liveness requires progress under stated conditions. “No seat is sold twice” is safety. “Every accepted valid booking eventually resolves” is a liveness-oriented obligation with environmental assumptions. A system that rejects all requests may protect the first but fail the second. Network models and failure thresholds can prevent unconditional progress guarantees. Write both properties, state what failures may block completion, and expose stuck work so operators can restore progress without violating safety.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · ordering models

    from mechanisms import vector_relation, lamport_receive
assert vector_relation([1,0], [0,1]) == "concurrent"
assert vector_relation([1,0], [1,2]) == "before"
assert lamport_receive(5, 9) == 10

    The first pair has no componentwise causal dominance; the second does. A Lamport timestamp smaller than another is not sufficient to prove causality in reverse. These values do not establish a consensus decision or real-time register behavior.

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.1

    Choose a replication model

    Prerequisites: Distributed Systems Fundamentals6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Three database replicas, one leader, and a network partition. Walk through elections, writes, acknowledgement rules, recovery, and potential data loss.

    This chapter examines choose a replication model through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    15.1.1 · Primary/replica architectures

    A primary/replica design gives one participant authority for a class of writes and copies its state elsewhere. It simplifies conflict ownership but requires promotion and protection against stale primaries. State who may accept writes and which failures preserve acknowledged data. Read replicas may provide older observations. A topology with one primary and two replicas is not a consensus specification; acknowledgment, persistence, election, membership, and recovery rules determine its actual guarantee.

    15.1.2 · Leader/follower replication

    Leader/follower replication sends an ordered stream from one leader to followers. Followers apply progress and can serve suitable reads or participate in failover under the protocol. Async followers may lag, while sync acknowledgment can increase latency. A follower that has received bytes but not durably stored the required record may not provide the intended crash-recovery protection. Track receive, persist, commit, and apply positions separately when the implementation distinguishes them.

    15.1.3 · Multi-leader replication

    Multi-leader replication allows writes at several authorities, often reducing local write latency or supporting disconnected regions. Concurrent writes can conflict and need resolution. Last-writer-wins based on unsynchronized timestamps can discard a meaningful update; deterministic convergence is not necessarily correct business merging. Use it for domains with justified conflict semantics, not an invariant that demands a single winner unless additional coordination exists. Observe replication loops, delete propagation, and recovery from prolonged disconnection.

    15.1.4 · Leaderless replication

    Leaderless designs let clients or coordinators contact several replicas and reconcile returned versions. Read repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy, and quorum configuration are separate mechanisms with implementation-specific effects. A successful response from two of three nodes does not establish linearizability without correct version and membership rules. Model concurrent writes and stale replica recovery. Choose this family when its availability, conflict, and operational contract fits the data; do not describe it as coordination-free for every possible operation.

    15.1.5 · Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

    Synchronous replication waits for specified acknowledgments before completing a write; asynchronous replication allows acknowledgment earlier. “Synchronous” must name whether an acknowledgment means received, durably stored, or applied. With async copying, loss of the only up-to-date owner can lose recent acknowledged writes. Waiting for independent durable replicas strengthens protection within the fault model but increases latency and may block during failure. Configuration is part of the application contract and must be tested during promotion.

    15.1.6 · Quorum-based systems

    A quorum is a permitted decision set under a protocol. Majority intersection can preserve evidence across elections or writes when persistence, voting, and membership rules hold. In a three-node fixed group, any two majorities share at least one node. That node must also obey rules about what it can acknowledge and later support. Quorum arithmetic without durable state or correct election eligibility is insufficient; a quorum is a component of a protocol, not a universal consistency switch.

    Architecture review · What does a region returning after failover have to prove before it can accept authoritative writes again?

    Use Workflow epoch checks for the local demonstration: epoch seven cannot complete after epoch eight owns the attempt. Explain why external storage must enforce its own fencing if old workers can still call it. A client-side lease flag cannot stop a resumed remote process.

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.2

    Raft and replicated state machines

    Prerequisites: 15.1 · Choose a replication model5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Three database replicas, one leader, and a network partition. Walk through elections, writes, acknowledgement rules, recovery, and potential data loss.

    This chapter examines raft and replicated state machines through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    15.2.1 · Consensus and replicated state machines

    Consensus makes nonfaulty participants agree on a decision sequence under specified assumptions. A replicated state machine applies the same ordered commands deterministically to maintain equivalent state. Nondeterministic choices such as current time or random IDs must be supplied or reconciled consistently rather than recomputed differently on each replica. Consensus does not automatically make external HTTP effects atomic with state-machine application. Keep those effects explicitly identified and deduplicated outside the replicated decision boundary.

    15.2.2 · Raft: terms, elections, log replication, commit

    Raft separates leader election, log replication, and safety. Terms identify election generations; a candidate needs a majority of votes and appropriate log freshness. Followers persist the protocol's required state. The leader replicates entries and advances commitment using Raft's rules, including the restriction on directly committing by majority counting to entries from its current term. This protects prior history through the protocol, not a generic “two acknowledgments always suffice” rule. Reads need a justified freshness mechanism too.

    15.2.3 · Paxos: conceptual foundations

    Paxos uses numbered proposals and intersecting majorities to ensure that once a value is chosen, later successful proposals preserve it under the protocol. Prepare and accept phases gather and carry forward required prior evidence. Multi-Paxos extends the approach for ordered decisions, often optimizing around a stable leader. This is a conceptual introduction, not executable consensus code. Production correctness depends on persistence, membership, retries, and liveness details; use a reviewed implementation rather than assembling a lock from the analogy.

    15.2.4 · Log ordering and durability

    A replicated log needs both an ordering rule and a durability rule. An entry present on one node is not necessarily committed, and an applied local state is not necessarily safe to expose as globally authoritative. Recovery must distinguish committed prefixes from conflicting uncommitted suffixes. Do not return success because bytes reached a follower unless the protocol says that event establishes the promised outcome. Observe commit and apply progress, and make snapshot installation preserve the same history assumptions.

    15.2.5 · Membership changes

    Membership changes alter which groups can make decisions. Replacing an old majority with a disjoint new majority in one step can allow conflicting histories. Protocols such as Raft use a coordinated transition, including overlapping quorum requirements in joint consensus. Learners may catch up before becoming voting members. A cluster-size setting is not merely an operations toggle: apply the supported membership protocol, preserve persistent identities, and test interruption during reconfiguration.

    Architecture review · What does a region returning after failover have to prove before it can accept authoritative writes again?

    Use Workflow epoch checks for the local demonstration: epoch seven cannot complete after epoch eight owns the attempt. Explain why external storage must enforce its own fencing if old workers can still call it. A client-side lease flag cannot stop a resumed remote process.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.3

    Fences, leases & failure detection

    Prerequisites: 15.2 · Raft and replicated state machines4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Three database replicas, one leader, and a network partition. Walk through elections, writes, acknowledgement rules, recovery, and potential data loss.

    This chapter examines fences, leases & failure detection through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    15.3.1 · Split-brain prevention and fencing tokens

    A fencing token is a monotonically ordered ownership epoch checked by the resource receiving an effect. Worker A holding token 7 can pause past its lease while B obtains token 8. When A resumes, the protected store must reject token 7. A token generated but never enforced at the side-effect boundary does not fence anything. The receiving resource must atomically compare and apply, and the design must account for operations already accepted before the newer owner appeared.

    15.3.2 · Failure detection

    Failure detection observes missing or delayed evidence and produces suspicion under timing assumptions. Short detection intervals can reduce failover delay but increase false suspicions during pauses or network congestion. The safety protocol must remain correct when suspicion is wrong. Separate detector tuning from authority transfer and resource fencing. A successful heartbeat also does not prove that the node can meet every business operation's deadline, so readiness and capacity signals remain useful alongside protocol heartbeats.

    15.3.3 · Strongly consistent metadata services

    Strongly consistent metadata services can coordinate configuration, ownership epochs, and small control-plane decisions. They are usually unsuitable as the high-volume store for every application payload. Cache safe configuration for serving where appropriate, and specify behavior when new ownership cannot be issued. A metadata outage can freeze deployments or leases while existing data paths continue; that distinction should appear in the failure model. Avoid making every request synchronously depend on a control plane unless its cost is justified.

    15.3.4 · Distributed locks and leases

    A lock grants a form of exclusive permission; a lease grants it for a time under clock and expiry assumptions. A paused owner may act after its lease ends, so resource-side fencing is often needed for correctness-critical effects. Releasing must verify owner identity rather than blindly delete another owner's lock. Lock acquisition and protected work are separate events. Prefer a single authoritative data transaction for a local invariant when it avoids an unnecessary distributed locking protocol.

    Architecture review · What does a region returning after failover have to prove before it can accept authoritative writes again?

    Use Workflow epoch checks for the local demonstration: epoch seven cannot complete after epoch eight owns the attempt. Explain why external storage must enforce its own fencing if old workers can still call it. A client-side lease flag cannot stop a resumed remote process.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Lock acquisition and protected work are separate events.

    Carry forward: Acquire lease with owner identity · Perform bounded protected work · Lease expires or owner pauses · Resource rejects stale owner through fencing.

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.4

    Conflicts, CRDTs & regional trade-offs

    Prerequisites: 15.3 · Fences, leases & failure detection4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Three database replicas, one leader, and a network partition. Walk through elections, writes, acknowledgement rules, recovery, and potential data loss.

    This chapter examines conflicts, crdts & regional trade-offs through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    15.4.1 · Conflict resolution and CRDT introduction

    CRDTs arrange updates and merges so replicas converge under stated algebraic and delivery assumptions. A grow-only set can merge by union; an observed-remove set needs metadata to distinguish observed additions from concurrent ones. Convergence does not enforce arbitrary invariants such as “stock never below zero.” Choose a type whose semantics match the domain, preserve required metadata, and bound tombstone growth or compaction safely. An explicit conflict review may be better for business edits without a natural automatic merge.

    15.4.2 · Multi-region replication trade-offs

    Regional replication must define write authority, conflict behavior, acknowledgment geography, and disaster recovery. A nearby async acknowledgment has different data-loss exposure from a cross-region durable quorum. During a partition, some operations may wait or reject while stale-tolerant reads continue. Reconnection requires catch-up and reconciliation before arbitrary old owners resume. Test failback as well as failover: restoring an old primary without epoch and history control can reintroduce conflicting state after the visible outage ends.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Pseudocode · three replicas, one partition

    A,B,C contain committed index 8
partition isolates old leader A
B and C elect eligible B in term 5
B appends index 9, term 5
B and C durably replicate index 9
Raft commit rule establishes committed prefix
A cannot acknowledge a new quorum-committed write alone
rejoin: A follows term 5 and repairs uncommitted suffix

    This trace assumes non-Byzantine members, correct durable protocol state, and a fixed three-voter configuration. It is not a replacement for the full Raft election and log safety rules or a production consensus implementation.

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.1

    Queues, logs & delivery boundaries

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus9 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an e-commerce checkout that coordinates payment, inventory reservation, shipment creation, and refund compensation.

    This chapter examines queues, logs & delivery boundaries through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    16.1.1 · Synchronous vs asynchronous communication

    Synchronous communication makes the caller wait for the result; asynchronous communication records or sends work whose completion is observed later. A receipt email can be deferred after an order commits, while payment acceptance may require a different response contract. Asynchrony moves waiting and failure handling into durable state and delivery protocols. A queue can absorb a short burst, but sustained arrival above completion still grows backlog. Define who owns accepted work after the initiating request ends.

    16.1.2 · Queues vs logs vs pub/sub

    A queue commonly distributes work among consumers; a retained log preserves an ordered append history for replay; pub/sub distributes publications to subscribers under its specific retention and acknowledgment semantics. Products combine these features, so check the actual contract. A consumer that needs replay after an outage cannot rely on an ephemeral subscription alone. Choose retention, partitioning, and consumer progress rules from recovery requirements rather than assuming every broker is a durable event history.

    16.1.3 · Producers, consumers, brokers

    Producers create messages, brokers accept or route them, and consumers interpret them. There are several distinct acknowledgments: producer acceptance, durable broker replication, consumer receipt, and completion of a business effect. Naming only “acknowledged” hides the boundary. Include stable message identity, schema version, ownership, and correlation metadata. A broker can be healthy while consumers repeatedly fail, so monitor end-to-end age and outcome rather than only broker uptime and enqueue rate.

    16.1.4 · Partitions, consumer groups, offsets

    Partitions provide ordered lanes in systems such as Kafka; consumer groups commonly distribute partitions among members, and offsets represent progress within a lane. Order is typically per partition, not across all partitions. Rebalancing can move ownership and cause work to repeat around an acknowledgment boundary. Commit offsets according to the effect contract and preserve stable keys for required ordering. One very hot partition can limit a group despite many idle consumers.

    16.1.5 · Delivery guarantees

    Delivery terminology must identify where messages and effects are counted. A broker can deliver at least once while a transactional consumer produces one local database effect through deduplication. An external provider can still receive repeated calls. Describe the full path: source acceptance, retention, retry, effect commit, and progress acknowledgment. Strong guarantees at one stage do not automatically compose into an end-to-end guarantee across independent systems and failures.

    16.1.6 · At-most-once and at-least-once processing

    At-most-once processing can acknowledge before an effect and lose work after a crash. It avoids certain duplicates at the cost of missing effects. It may suit disposable telemetry under a deliberate loss budget, but not an order that has been promised durable processing. The term does not imply “always one”; zero is allowed. Specify whether the guarantee concerns delivery attempts, processing starts, or committed results because different boundaries can produce different counts.

    At-least-once processing retries until acknowledged under retention and recovery assumptions, so duplicates are possible. Commit a durable effect before acknowledging and make repetition safe. A crash after commit but before acknowledgment replays the record. A uniqueness constraint on event identity within the same local transaction as the effect can prevent duplicate local changes. If the transaction marks processed before making an unprotected remote call, it can lose that call; the effect boundary matters.

    16.1.7 · Exactly-once processing within defined boundaries

    Exactly-once claims require a precise boundary. A transactional stream processor may atomically couple consumed progress and produced records within its supported system. That does not include an arbitrary email server or payment provider unless another protocol covers the side effect. Idempotency can give a single relevant effect for repeated attempts under a retention and identity contract; it does not mean execution started only once. Name failures and recovery assumptions instead of using the phrase as a universal broker property.

    16.1.8 · Ordering guarantees

    Ordering can mean publication order, per-key log order, consumer start order, or effect-commit order. Parallel processing can preserve one while changing another. If account operations must apply sequentially, partition or coordinate by account and do not acknowledge later changes as if earlier ones completed. Poison messages require a policy: skipping can restore progress while breaking the business sequence. Use sequence numbers and explicit gap handling where the domain depends on ordered effects.

    16.1.9 · Consumer acknowledgements

    A consumer acknowledgment permits the broker to advance or remove delivery state according to the protocol. If acknowledgment precedes a required effect, a crash can lose work; if it follows, a crash can repeat work. There is no magical placement that atomically covers an unrelated external system. Use local transactions, inbox/outbox records, provider operation keys, and reconciliation as appropriate. Keep acknowledgment deadlines compatible with processing time and lease extension rules so healthy long jobs are not repeatedly redelivered.

    Architecture review · Can one workflow be exactly once at a broker boundary but still send two emails? Specify the boundaries.

    The example records two deliveries but one counter effect. Deduplication identity and effect commit share a transaction. If an external email or payment is substituted for the counter, the local inbox no longer establishes one external effect; use the provider contract and reconciliation.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Use local transactions, inbox/outbox records, provider operation keys, and reconciliation as appropriate.

    Carry forward: Effect starts · Effect commits · Consumer acknowledges · Lost acknowledgment triggers safe replay.

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.2

    Retries, poison messages & idempotence

    Prerequisites: 16.1 · Queues, logs & delivery boundaries4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an e-commerce checkout that coordinates payment, inventory reservation, shipment creation, and refund compensation.

    This chapter examines retries, poison messages & idempotence through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    16.2.1 · Retries and dead-letter queues

    Retry transient failures with a bounded policy and delay; dead-letter persistent failures with context and a path for repair. A dead-letter queue is not a completed business outcome. Include original identity, attempt count, failure reason, and source version, then alert or reconcile unresolved important work. Replaying a repaired record must preserve deduplication and ordering rules. An unbounded retry loop can block a partition or overwhelm a permanently invalid downstream request.

    16.2.2 · Poison messages

    A poison message repeatedly fails because of malformed data, incompatible schema, or an invariant violation. Distinguish it from a temporary dependency failure so retries do not waste the same resources forever. Quarantine it with evidence and decide whether dependent messages must wait. A parser bug can make an entire valid historical schema look poisonous; inspect error distributions and replay samples before discarding records. Privacy rules apply to diagnostic payloads retained in quarantine.

    16.2.3 · Idempotent consumers

    An idempotent consumer records event identity and its relevant local effect atomically. INSERT processed(event_id) under uniqueness and the corresponding state update must share one transaction if they protect the same invariant. A duplicate then returns the already established outcome. Retain identity long enough for permitted replay and delayed delivery. This protects local effects only; calling an external provider still requires its operation key or reconciliation. Deduplicating only in volatile memory fails after restart.

    16.2.4 · Event sourcing

    Event sourcing stores domain events as the authoritative history from which state is derived. It supports audit and reconstruction when event semantics remain interpretable, but adds schema evolution, correction, replay, and privacy obligations. A snapshot accelerates reconstruction and must identify its event position. Do not replay external side effects while merely rebuilding state. Append-only history is not automatically a legally sufficient ledger or an authorization model; domain and operational constraints still need design.

    Architecture review · Can one workflow be exactly once at a broker boundary but still send two emails? Specify the boundaries.

    The example records two deliveries but one counter effect. Deduplication identity and effect commit share a transaction. If an external email or payment is substituted for the counter, the local inbox no longer establishes one external effect; use the provider contract and reconciliation.

    Use the failure histories and assumptions above to defend an answer. Distinguish the local mechanism demonstrated here from the full system boundary in the linked complete design.

    CHECK THE BOUNDARY

    Do not replay external side effects while merely rebuilding state.

    Carry forward: Append domain event · Fold events into current state · Snapshot records position · Replay rebuilds state without repeating effects.

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.3

    Event sourcing, CQRS & the outbox

    Prerequisites: 16.2 · Retries, poison messages & idempotence4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an e-commerce checkout that coordinates payment, inventory reservation, shipment creation, and refund compensation.

    This chapter examines event sourcing, cqrs & the outbox through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    16.3.1 · CQRS

    CQRS separates command and query responsibilities or models when their requirements differ. An order command model can enforce transitions while a read projection provides a convenient customer history. The projection may lag, so clients need a read-after-write policy. CQRS does not require event sourcing, independent databases, or microservices. Its additional models and synchronization are justified when they simplify real complexity, not when a straightforward CRUD application already satisfies its access patterns.

    16.3.2 · Transactional outbox

    A transactional outbox records state changes and publication intent in the same local transaction. A relay later publishes pending intents and marks progress. If it publishes then crashes before marking, it can publish again, so consumers still deduplicate. The pattern closes a local database-to-publication gap; it does not make arbitrary subscribers part of that transaction. Use stable event IDs, retryable relay progress, retention, and reconciliation for intents that remain unprocessed too long.

    16.3.3 · Sagas and compensating transactions

    A saga coordinates local transactions and compensating actions across ownership boundaries. Inventory reservation, payment authorization, and shipment creation cannot be treated as one ordinary local transaction. On failure, compensation might release stock or request a refund, but it can fail and may not perfectly reverse the original action. Persist workflow state and compensation progress. Distinguish recoverable intermediate states from final success or failure, and reconcile with external systems after uncertain responses.

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.4

    Sagas, durable work & reconciliation

    Prerequisites: 16.3 · Event sourcing, CQRS & the outbox6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Design an e-commerce checkout that coordinates payment, inventory reservation, shipment creation, and refund compensation.

    This chapter examines sagas, durable work & reconciliation through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    16.4.1 · Choreography vs orchestration

    Choreography lets participants react to events without one central workflow coordinator; orchestration stores and directs the workflow explicitly. Choreography can reduce centralized coupling but makes end-to-end progress harder to see. Orchestration clarifies ownership and retries while introducing a coordinator and workflow schema to operate. Neither eliminates participant failures. Choose based on workflow complexity, auditability, change ownership, and compensation needs, and maintain a correlation identity through every step.

    16.4.2 · Workflow engines

    A workflow engine persists execution progress and resumes work after failures under its programming model. It can manage timers, retries, and human waits, but activities calling external systems can still execute more than once around acknowledgment gaps. Understand deterministic replay, versioning, activity identity, and cancellation rules of the chosen implementation. An engine is a tool for durable orchestration, not proof that every external side effect or business invariant has become exactly once.

    16.4.3 · Durable job execution

    Durable jobs have a persistent identity, input reference, state, attempt history, and ownership protocol. A worker should record completion under the current attempt or fencing epoch so a stale worker cannot overwrite a newer result. Store large payloads outside the queue and validate input version before work. Retry does not mean unlimited recomputation: set budgets and surface terminal or review states. A process-local background task is not durable merely because the request returned 202.

    16.4.4 · Scheduling, leases, and worker coordination

    Scheduling combines a durable due-time record with worker coordination. A scheduler claims due work using an atomic transition or lease and creates a stable run identity such as (schedule_id,occurrence). Clock changes, missed periods, overlapping runs, and failover need explicit policy. A lease can expire while the old worker runs, so protect effects with fencing or idempotency at their resource. Exactly one scheduler process is not a substitute for a recoverable occurrence protocol.

    16.4.5 · Backpressure and replay

    Backpressure controls admission or producer progress when consumers cannot keep up; replay deliberately revisits retained input. Replaying at full historical speed can overload live dependencies and delay current work. Give replay its own rate and capacity budget, preserve source identity, and isolate side effects. Retention must cover the recovery horizon. Queue length alone is not enough: monitor oldest age, per-key blockage, and meaningful completion rates so a seemingly busy pipeline does not conceal stuck business outcomes.

    16.4.6 · Reconciliation after partial failure

    Reconciliation compares intended and observed outcomes after partial failure. A payment marked pending locally may already be charged at the provider; query by stable operation identity and repair the local state rather than blindly charging again. Reconciliation must itself be idempotent, authorized, and observable. Run it periodically and during incident recovery, tracking unresolved discrepancies with age and ownership. It is an essential protocol stage, not an admission that the normal path can ignore persistence or validation.

    Worked implementation · connect the unit

    Python · duplicate delivery, one local effect

    from mechanisms import open_demo_store, consume_local_event
db = open_demo_store()
assert consume_local_event(db, "E1", "orders")
assert not consume_local_event(db, "E1", "orders")
assert db.execute("SELECT value FROM counters").fetchone()[0] == 1
db.close()

    The event ID and local effect share a transaction. Replacing the counter with an external provider call invalidates this one-local-effect argument unless the external boundary has its own protocol.

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.1

    Failure domains & redundancy

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A downstream payment provider becomes unavailable during peak traffic. Demonstrate the failure cascade and progressively introduce resilience mechanisms.

    This chapter examines failure domains & redundancy through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    17.1.1 · Failure domains and fault isolation

    A failure domain groups elements exposed to a common cause: a process, host, zone, dependency, or administrative action. Isolate critical functions so one overload or crash cannot consume every resource. Two workers sharing one disk and credential source may fail together even in different processes. Map correlations and test them. Isolation has a cost in duplicate capacity, network calls, and operating work, so apply it according to the harm and recovery objectives of each failure.

    17.1.2 · Availability vs durability

    Availability concerns useful serving behavior; durability concerns retained committed state under stated failures. A database can remain durable while unavailable during recovery. A stateless application can return 200 while silently dropping writes. Specify and observe both properties independently. Backups, replication, timeouts, and failover affect different parts of the contract. Do not promise a “reliable service” without explaining eligible requests, required outcomes, data-loss tolerance, and the time window or failure model being evaluated.

    17.1.3 · Redundancy

    Redundancy adds spare components or copies, but their usefulness depends on independence, capacity, detection, and state correctness. If two instances each run at 70% and one fails, the other cannot absorb all traffic without overload. Plan reduced-capacity behavior or reserve appropriate headroom. Shared configuration mistakes can disable all replicas simultaneously. Redundancy should be paired with tested traffic movement and recovery, rather than counted as a number of boxes in an architecture picture.

    17.1.4 · Active-active vs active-passive

    Active-active serves from multiple locations or owners; active-passive keeps a standby for takeover. The choice concerns a particular function: applications may be active-active while a database has one write leader. Active-passive simplifies some authority decisions but can reveal cold-start and drift problems during failover. Active-active adds routing, coordination, or conflict complexity. Define failure detection, promotion, fencing, capacity, and failback for either model; a standby that has never restored usable state is unproven protection.

    Architecture review · How can a disaster exercise pass infrastructure checks yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Compute 3^4 = 81 potential attempts for four independently retrying layers. Introduce one end-to-end retry budget, bounded waits, admission, and channel isolation. Do not use a false payment approval as a fallback. Verify recovery behavior and unresolved business state after the provider returns.

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.2

    Retries, circuit breakers & isolation

    Prerequisites: 17.1 · Failure domains & redundancy6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A downstream payment provider becomes unavailable during peak traffic. Demonstrate the failure cascade and progressively introduce resilience mechanisms.

    This chapter examines retries, circuit breakers & isolation through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    17.2.1 · Timeouts

    Timeouts bound waiting and resource ownership. Use an overall request deadline plus sensible stage limits for connection, pool acquisition, and operations. A timeout should trigger cleanup or cancellation where possible, but does not prove a remote action failed. Choosing every timeout independently can let downstream work outlive the caller's useful window. Propagate remaining time and avoid beginning expensive work that cannot finish within it. Record timeout stage to distinguish queueing from execution failures.

    17.2.2 · Retries, exponential backoff, jitter

    Retries can recover transient faults but spend capacity. Use bounded attempts, exponential backoff, jitter, and error classification, with a stable identity for effects. A permanent validation failure should not be retried unchanged. Respect downstream retry guidance where applicable, but do not let a large Retry-After exceed the business operation's lifecycle unnoticed. Retry policies belong to the end-to-end design; one safe retry layer is often better than many independently aggressive layers.

    17.2.3 · Retry storms

    A retry storm amplifies an outage when many callers repeat work against a struggling dependency. Three attempts at four nested layers can produce 81 downstream attempts per original intent. Random delay reduces synchronization, but an attempt budget and admission control are also needed. Preserve goodput by rejecting excess work and suppressing redundant attempts. Monitor original business intents separately from attempts so apparent traffic growth during an outage is not mistaken for healthy user demand.

    17.2.4 · Circuit breakers

    A circuit breaker tracks dependency failures and temporarily rejects or redirects calls under a policy. Common states are closed, open, and half-open, with bounded probes to test recovery. It prevents futile waiting but does not repair the dependency or decide domain correctness. A fallback that returns a fabricated payment approval is unsafe. Make failure classification, probe concurrency, and recovery thresholds explicit, and avoid every instance probing simultaneously after the same interval.

    17.2.5 · Bulkheads

    Bulkheads partition resources so one class of work cannot consume everything. Separate pools for payment authorization and optional receipt delivery can keep checkout viable when email stalls. Pool sizing must include shared limits such as database connections and host memory; separate thread pools alone do not isolate every dependency. Over-isolation can waste spare capacity. Choose boundaries by failure harm and observe saturation and rejection in each partition, not only fleet-level averages.

    17.2.6 · Rate limiting

    Rate limiting protects a boundary from excessive traffic under a defined identity and burst policy. A token bucket permits bounded bursts while enforcing a refill rate; a queue-based shaper changes timing rather than simply rejecting. For multi-tenant services, combine per-tenant fairness with global capacity protection. A limiter depending on an unavailable remote store needs a deliberate fail-open, fail-closed, or local-budget policy. Each choice affects abuse risk and availability, so test the failure mode explicitly.

Do not use a false payment approval as a fallback. Verify recovery behavior and unresolved business state after the provider returns.

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.3

    Shed load and degrade deliberately

    Prerequisites: 17.2 · Retries, circuit breakers & isolation4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A downstream payment provider becomes unavailable during peak traffic. Demonstrate the failure cascade and progressively introduce resilience mechanisms.

    This chapter examines shed load and degrade deliberately through concrete mechanisms, state snapshots, failure cases, and alternatives.

    17.3.1 · Load shedding

    Load shedding rejects lower-value or excessive work before resources are exhausted. A service may stop recommendations while preserving order status and payment reconciliation. Decide priorities from business meaning, and avoid spending expensive computation only to reject at the end. Shedding should return a clear outcome with bounded retry behavior. It improves useful completion under overload, but cannot make an unsustainable workload sustainable indefinitely; scaling, workload reduction, or a changed objective may still be needed.

    17.3.2 · Graceful degradation

    Graceful degradation preserves a useful subset of behavior under failure. Showing product descriptions without recommendations can be acceptable; displaying stale available inventory as permission to sell may not be. Define which data may be stale, which actions must pause, and how users see the limitation. Test degraded paths because rarely used fallbacks can fail when needed. Degradation is a product and correctness decision, not simply catching every exception and returning a default value.

    17.3.3 · Fallbacks

    A fallback substitutes an alternative behavior with an explicit contract. A cached help page can replace a failed content request; a default account balance cannot replace a failed ledger lookup. Fallbacks can create load elsewhere and can mask a prolonged incident. Bound their freshness and duration, signal degraded operation, and check security scope. A second provider is not transparent if its semantics, operation identities, or reconciliation process differ from the first.

    17.3.4 · Health checking

    Health checks should answer a useful local question and be bounded. Restarting a process because a shared provider is down can create a restart storm without repairing the provider. Readiness may stop new work while allowing in-flight operations to finish. Liveness should avoid external dependencies that can fail independently. Include startup and warmup behavior, and distinguish “process responds to probe” from “critical business operations meet their objectives.” Probe success is evidence, not a complete reliability guarantee.

Do not use a false payment approval as a fallback. Verify recovery behavior and unresolved business state after the provider returns.
