    Why does cost per attempt sometimes conceal cost per useful outcome?

    Cost per request can obscure the business outcome if retries or failures inflate the denominator. Prefer cost per successful order, delivered document, or another meaningful unit, while still analyzing technical costs. With an assumed monthly cost of 3000 units and 150000 successful outcomes, unit cost is 0.02. If half the attempts fail, dividing by all attempts understates the cost of useful work. Define period, allocation, and included operating expenses.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / C5

    What should a useful architecture fitness function protect?

    Architecture fitness functions continuously test required properties such as allowed imports, tenant-scoped queries, API compatibility, or recovery time. A useful function protects a reasoned architectural characteristic without freezing every incidental class relationship. Some properties need runtime drills or manual review rather than a static rule. Keep tests aligned with current decisions and update them when an ADR legitimately changes the architecture. Passing a collection of checks is evidence for their scope, not a universal architecture certification.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / S1

    An index fixes the actual slow query. Why might sharding have been a worse first intervention?

    Tuning improves an implementation within its architecture; an architectural change alters ownership, placement, or major interaction. An index, batch size, or shorter transaction may resolve a bottleneck with less migration risk than sharding. Conversely, an unavoidably centralized invariant can require a different business or partitioning model. Measure before and after, and count correctness, operations, and migration cost alongside speed. The most sophisticated topology is not automatically the most defensible intervention.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / S2

    The process is only killed before starting work. Which dangerous failure windows remain untested?

    Fault injection tests behavior when a dependency is slow, unavailable, inconsistent, or interrupted. Place faults at meaningful boundaries: after database commit but before acknowledgment, during partition transfer, or after a worker lease expires. Killing a process only before work starts misses the dangerous windows. Define acceptable outcomes and stop conditions. Combine fault evidence with data reconciliation; an application that recovers request serving while silently losing jobs has not passed the full business contract.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / S3

    Source and destination have equal row counts but different ownership. Why did the validation miss a bug?

    Data validation compares source and destination identities, versions, aggregates, and domain invariants. Row counts alone cannot detect swapped ownership, stale updates, or equal-count omissions and duplicates. For a ledger, validate balanced postings and unique external operation identity; for a search index, compare source version and deletion state. Run checks after migration, replay, and recovery. Sampling can reduce cost but weakens the claim, so state whether evidence covers all records or only a sample.

    UNIT 21 / D1

    Design or debug the running system: Compare three architectures using explicit fictional costs and equal requirement checks.

    cost_options() totals 371, 551, and 1402 fictional monthly units. These are cost inputs only, not measured capacities or reliability. Compare each with original latency, failure, correctness, and operating constraints; reject an infeasible cheap option before ranking cost efficiency. Begin with the smallest correct boundary and identify an observable failure of the naive alternative.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / I1

    Compare three architectures using explicit fictional costs and equal requirement checks. Include a counterexample and a corrected result.

    cost_options() totals 371, 551, and 1402 fictional monthly units. These are cost inputs only, not measured capacities or reliability. Compare each with original latency, failure, correctness, and operating constraints; reject an infeasible cheap option before ranking cost efficiency.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / T1

    What evidence would justify accepting a more expensive architecture as the simpler complete operating system?

    A defensible answer must state the changed contract, the authoritative owner, and the failure history before choosing a mechanism. Validate the design against its original requirements using a traceable evidence matrix. Every promise should identify a test, measurement, review, or unresolved assumption. Compare functional behavior, latency distributions, capacity, recovery, security, cost, and operational burden under the stated workload. A diagram review and a load test provide different evidence. If a target remains unmeasured, label it as an objective rather than reporting it as achieved. This closes the loop from design hypothesis to defensible engineering decision. A component name or a claim that more replicas solve it is insufficient; show how the proposed history remains valid under the stated failure.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 22 · End-to-End Design, Architecture Reviews, and Evolution

    UNIT 22 / C1

    Why do the twelve designs use different authoritative and derived state boundaries?

    Creation and code ownership require an atomic uniqueness boundary; management reads should meet the chosen read-after-write contract. Redirects may permit bounded stale targets only if revocation and expiry requirements allow it. Analytics can be eventually processed with stable event identities. Do not describe the whole system as simply eventual: the mapping insertion and the click count have different obligations. Accepted post identity and deletion state need strong local transactional handling. Candidate projections and engagement counts can be eventually refreshed. Read-your-writes for an author's own post may require a direct-source overlay. Authorization is not allowed to become weaker merely because candidates are stale. State which parts of the feed are snapshots and which are revalidated at every serving operation.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C2

    Why are a chat persistence receipt and a human read receipt different?

    Send a message to an authorized conversation, retain it durably, deliver online updates, reconnect and fetch missed messages, and expose a meaningful receipt model. Support one-to-one and bounded group conversations. Presence is approximate and ephemeral. Define sent, persisted, delivered-to-device, and read as different states rather than promising that opening a WebSocket makes every message read by a person. Provide monotonic per-conversation sequence under the selected authority, read-after-write for sender confirmation, and replayable catch-up. Cross-conversation ordering is unnecessary unless a product requirement says otherwise. Device delivery is at least retryable and can duplicate frames; clients deduplicate by message identity. Presence and read indicators may be eventually updated but should not move backward under their defined receipt model.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C3

    Why can a scheduler lease not guarantee a single external execution?

    Schedule advancement and occurrence creation need atomicity and uniqueness. Worker delivery can be at least once. Conditional completion under the current epoch prevents stale local results; idempotency at the side-effect boundary or enforced fencing protects business effects. A lease by itself cannot prove exactly-once execution. Explicitly define misfire and overlap policies instead of letting timing races decide whether a missed occurrence runs.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C4

    Why does a collaborative editor need more than eventual string equality?

    OT transforms concurrent operations against the relevant ordered context; an insertion can shift another insertion's position. CRDTs choose merge semantics that converge under their algorithm's assumptions, often using stable element identifiers and ordering. For two concurrent inserts X and Y after the same element, replicas need the same tie-break rule. Neither acronym supplies all intent or rich-text semantics. Authorization and durable acknowledgment remain separate from convergence. Authorize every sync and operation, not only opening the document page. Recheck membership according to a defined revocation policy for long-lived sessions and offline reconnect. Restrict exports and snapshots, avoid leaking content through presence or logs, and validate protocol inputs. If end-to-end encryption is required, explain how server-side search, validation, history, and access revocation change; transport TLS alone is not that guarantee.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C5

    Why is a document-processing complete state inadequate without provenance and publication evidence?

    Failures include incomplete uploads, corrupt files, malicious content, worker crash after output write, duplicate stage delivery, incompatible model output, stale completion, review races, missing lineage, and deletion during processing. Stable artifacts and epoch-checked transitions prevent stale overwrite. Quarantine invalid outputs with reasons. A document marked complete without usable authorized output or source evidence is a failed workflow even if no worker raised an exception. Measure accepted bytes, stage queue age, compute time, retries, stale completion rejects, validation failures, review backlog, provenance completeness, publication lag, tenant denials, and deletion progress. Track automated quality with an appropriate labeled evaluation rather than presenting confidence as accuracy. Link one document's source, workflow, attempt, model, output, and reviewer through stable identities and privacy-safe telemetry.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / S1

    A booking payment succeeds after its seat hold expires. What outcomes are safe?

    Claim seats atomically with the reservation, commit, and return its deadline. Payment workflow submits a stable provider operation. Confirmation checks a still-valid authorized transition and commits ticket issuance plus reservation/seat state. If payment succeeds after expiry, follow a defined recovery policy such as reacquisition if safe or refund; do not silently issue a ticket for a now-owned seat. Expiry uses conditional versioned release. Two users reading available must not both win. A process can crash after reservation commit but before reply; idempotency must recover it. Payment can succeed after the hold expires, and stale expiry work can arrive after a renewal or new reservation. Version-checked transitions and reconciliation prevent these from corrupting ownership. Email delivery failure must not imply ticket issuance failed if the ticket already committed.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / S2

    A payment provider charges, the local process dies, and a client retries. What prevents a second logical charge?

    Commit intent and operation identity, dispatch a stable provider key, then record authoritative response or uncertainty. Apply settlement or capture evidence through an idempotent transition that creates balanced ledger postings once. Verified callbacks can arrive late or before a synchronous response and must not regress state incorrectly. Reconciliation queries stable provider references and repairs discrepancies without blindly resubmitting a charge. Deduplication, payment-state changes, and required local postings need appropriate atomicity. Provider effects are outside that local boundary and rely on provider identity and reconciliation contracts. Exactly-once local posting can be enforced with uniqueness and transaction semantics; exactly-once external execution is not implied. Refunds have their own lifecycle and may not perfectly reverse timing, fees, or downstream business consequences.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / S3

    A deleted document has an old extraction worker still running. What must prevent publication?

    Verify upload and source digest, create a stable workflow, classify, extract, validate schema and semantic checks, record evidence, and either publish or request review. Human decisions create a new validated result version and publication intent. Each stage conditionally commits under its current attempt epoch. Reprocessing creates a new run over an identified source version rather than mutating old provenance. Deletion cancels or blocks inappropriate later publication. Source versions are immutable, workflow transitions and review decisions commit atomically where required, and derived artifacts identify their exact inputs. Stage delivery can repeat, but output identity and conditional commit make local progress safe. Search may lag publication while enforcing access. External model calls can be uncertain or nondeterministic; retain relevant version and request identity, validate output, and avoid claiming reproducibility beyond the actual model contract.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / D1

    Review the URL shortener at 100000 redirects/s with a cold cache and immediate revocation requirement.

    At 10000 redirects/s and an assumed 90% cache hit ratio, nominal authoritative reads are 1000/s before coalescing and retries. Peak 100000 redirects/s implies 10000 misses/s if the ratio holds. Peak response traffic at 500 bytes is 50 MB/s before transport overhead. Failure planning must include a cold-cache case, not only this nominal miss rate. A code collision must cause an atomic uniqueness failure and retry, not overwrite the prior target. A cache outage must not flood storage without admission control. A lost creation reply must replay the committed operation result. A stale cache may serve a revoked link unless its policy limits that exposure. Analytics failure should reduce analytics freshness rather than redirect availability. The weakest assumptions are cache freshness during revocation, cold-cache origin capacity, and global uniqueness after partitioning. Review them with a revoke-under-load test, a full cache-loss exercise, and a forced code-collision test spanning the actual ownership boundary. Prefer an explicit bounded-degradation policy over a claim that cache replication automatically solves all three concerns.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / I1

    Choose one case and implement its final challenge with failure injection and an explicit invariant.

    Each case ends with a specific miniature implementation challenge. Use stable identities, test the stated failure window, and compare the result with the case invariant. For the included examples, run verify_mechanisms.py and inspect the outbox and ledger fixtures. A success-only demonstration is insufficient because it does not exercise the proposed recovery boundary.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / T1

    You may fund only one improvement in a small platform: another region, tested restores, or stronger retry and reconciliation. How do you decide?

    There is no universal winner. Start from the most harmful demonstrated or unacceptable failure and the original requirements. Another region cannot repair a lost idempotency history, and retries cannot restore a destroyed sole copy. Tested restores establish only their tested recovery scope. Compare risk reduction, cost, staffing, and the evidence each choice would produce; record the decision and revisit trigger.

    Error budget

    Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton

    Failure domains and fault isolation

    Fallbacks

    Feature flags

    Gathering and prioritizing requirements

    Graceful degradation
    Graceful degradation preserves a useful subset of behavior under failure. Read the lesson →

    Health checking

    Health checks and failover

    Hexagonal/Ports and Adapters

    Hot partitions and skew

    How databases store and retrieve records

    Immutable infrastructure

    In-process vs distributed caches

    Incident response

    Index selection and query optimization
    An index speeds selected access paths while consuming space and write work. Read the lesson →
    Indexing pipelines
    An indexing pipeline transforms authoritative content into searchable representations. Read the lesson →
    Infrastructure as Code
    Infrastructure as Code describes desired resources and policy in reviewable form. Read the lesson →
    Infrastructure ownership and managed services
    A managed service transfers selected tasks, not business responsibility. Read the lesson →
    Interface
    The operations and data forms exposed to a collaborator; behavior needs an accompanying contract. Read the lesson →
    Interfaces and contracts
    A gateway interface must specify currency, amount units, timeouts, duplicate identity, and error meaning. Read the lesson →
    Invariant
    A condition required to hold in every valid system state. Read the lesson →

    Inversion of Control means some control is delegated to a framework or external coordinator: an event loop invokes your callback, or a host constructs your request handler. Read the lesson →
    IP addresses, ports, sockets, routing

    Isolation levels and implementation differences

    Iterator
    An iterator exposes traversal without requiring clients to know the collection representation. Read the lesson →
    Key management and rotation
    Key management includes generation, storage, access, rotation, versioning, backup, and destruction. Read the lesson →
    Key-value databases
    A key-value store maps keys to values under a defined read/write contract. Read the lesson →
    Kubernetes fundamentals
    Kubernetes reconciles declared objects with cluster state through its control plane and node agents. Read the lesson →
    L4 vs L7 load balancing

    Latency

    Latency caused by network round trips
    Round trips create a latency floor even before useful computation. Read the lesson →
    Latency, throughput, QPS, RPS, TPS
    Latency measures elapsed time; throughput measures completed work per time interval. Read the lesson →

    LLD
    Low-Level Design: a common view of internal modules, types, interfaces, algorithms, and collaboration. Read the lesson →

    Memory visibility and happens-before relationships

    Metadata vs binary data

    Modular monoliths

    Modularity

    Multi-region strategies

    Multipart and resumable uploads

    Strategy
    A strategy supplies an interchangeable algorithm behind a stable behavioral contract, such as channel selection or fee calculation. Read the lesson →
    Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor
    Behavioral patterns organize decisions and coordination. Read the lesson →
    Stream processing fundamentals
    Stream processing maintains results over ongoing events using windows, keys, and state. Read the lesson →
    Streaming APIs and long-running operations
    A long-running operation can return an operation resource and let clients poll or subscribe for progress. Read the lesson →
    Strong consistency and eventual consistency
    Strong consistency is often used informally for linearizable behavior, but must be defined in context. Read the lesson →
    Strongly consistent metadata services
    Strongly consistent metadata services can coordinate configuration, ownership epochs, and small control-plane decisions. Read the lesson →
    Structured logging
    Structured logging uses named fields with stable meanings rather than relying only on free-form messages. Read the lesson →
    Supply-chain security
    Supply-chain security covers dependencies, build tools, artifacts, deployment permissions, and update paths. Read the lesson →
    Sustainability and resource efficiency
    Resource efficiency includes avoiding idle work, unnecessary transfer, redundant computation, and over-retention. Read the lesson →
    Synchronous vs asynchronous communication
    Synchronous communication makes the caller wait for the result; asynchronous communication records or sends work whose completion is observed later. Read the lesson →
    Synchronous vs asynchronous execution
    Synchronous execution ties the caller's progress to completing an operation; asynchronous execution separates initiation from later completion. Read the lesson →
    Synchronous vs asynchronous replication
    Synchronous replication waits for specified acknowledgments before completing a write; asynchronous replication allows acknowledgment earlier. Read the lesson →
    Tail latency analysis
    Tail analysis examines distributions and critical dependencies rather than only means. Read the lesson →
    Tail latency and latency budgets
    A request's tail can be dominated by the slowest dependency. Read the lesson →
    TCP vs UDP vs QUIC
    TCP supplies an ordered reliable byte stream; it preserves bytes, not application-message boundaries. Read the lesson →
    Technical vs business boundaries
    Technical boundaries group by mechanism, such as controllers or databases; business boundaries group coherent capabilities, such as orders or fulfillment. Read the lesson →
    Tell, Don't Ask
    Tell, Don't Ask encourages sending an intention to the state owner. Read the lesson →
    Template Method
    A template method fixes an algorithm skeleton and permits selected steps to vary, commonly through inheritance. Read the lesson →
    Testability and design for change
    Testability follows controllable inputs, visible outcomes, and explicit effects. Read the lesson →
    The fallacies of distributed computing
    The fallacies of distributed computing warn against assuming reliable networks, zero latency, infinite bandwidth, static topology, free transport, homogeneous infrastructure, automatic security, or one administrator. Read the lesson →
    Thread pools and worker pools
    A worker pool caps simultaneously executing jobs, while a bounded queue caps waiting jobs. Read the lesson →
    Thread safety and immutability
    Thread safety is a behavioral property under a stated concurrent-use contract. Read the lesson →
    Threat modeling
    Threat modeling starts from assets, actors, trust boundaries, and abuse goals. Read the lesson →
    Throughput
    Completed work per unit time under a specified workload and success definition. Read the lesson →
    Time, clocks, and event ordering
    Wall clocks support timestamps and scheduling but can drift, jump, or be adjusted. Read the lesson →
    Time-series databases
    Time-series data combines timestamps, measurements, and dimensions. Read the lesson →
    Timeouts
    Timeouts bound waiting and resource ownership. Read the lesson →
    TLS and HTTPS
    TLS authenticates peers according to the configured trust model and protects traffic integrity and confidentiality. Read the lesson →
    Trace IDs, span IDs, context propagation
    Trace IDs identify a trace, span IDs identify individual spans, and propagation carries the relevant context across boundaries. Read the lesson →
    Trade-off
    A choice among competing consequences evaluated against requirements and assumptions. Read the lesson →
    Transaction commit and rollback
    Commit establishes a transaction's accepted outcome according to the engine's protocol; rollback abandons its uncommitted work. Read the lesson →
    Transactional outbox
    Recording a state change and publication intent in one local transaction, then relaying the intent; duplicate delivery still requires handling. Read the lesson →
    Transactions across multiple operations
    A business operation spanning several statements needs one deliberate atomic boundary if its invariant requires all-or-nothing changes. Read the lesson →
    Transient, scoped, singleton, and framework-specific lifetimes
    Transient means a resolution creates a new instance; scoped means instances are reused within a defined scope; singleton means reuse within the container or application boundary specified by the framework. Read the lesson →
    Trust boundaries
    A trust boundary changes the confidence or authority granted to input. Read the lesson →
    Trust boundary
    A point across which identity, privilege, or confidence in input changes. Read the lesson →
    TTL and cache expiration
    A TTL bounds intended residence after insertion, not necessarily the age of the underlying fact when inserted. Read the lesson →
    Twelve-Factor App principles
    The Twelve-Factor App is methodology for service-oriented application operation: explicit dependencies and configuration, backing services, stateless processes where appropriate, logs as event streams, and related deployment practices. Read the lesson →
    Unit of Work
    A Unit of Work groups local changes under one commit and tracks their ownership. Read the lesson →
    Unit, integration, contract, end-to-end, and performance tests
    Unit tests isolate local behavior; integration tests verify real collaborators; contract tests verify boundary expectations; end-to-end tests exercise complete journeys. Read the lesson →
    User journeys and workload characteristics
    Users do not generate a constant stream of identical requests. Read the lesson →
    Vector indexes: introductory architecture only
    A vector index supports similarity search over numerical embeddings. Read the lesson →
    Vertical vs horizontal scaling
    Vertical scaling increases resources of one node; horizontal scaling adds nodes. Read the lesson →
    Virtual machines vs containers
    A virtual machine presents virtualized hardware with its guest operating system; containers commonly isolate processes while sharing a host kernel. Read the lesson →
    Visitor
    A visitor adds operations over a known structure by dispatching on element type. Read the lesson →
    Webhooks and delivery acknowledgments
    A webhook is an asynchronous request to another party. Read the lesson →
    WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and polling
    Polling repeatedly asks for updates; server-sent events stream server-to-client events over HTTP; WebSockets support bidirectional messaging after protocol setup. Read the lesson →
    What data storage must guarantee
    Storage choices begin with promises: what is accepted, when it is committed, how it can be read, and which failures it survives. Read the lesson →
    What makes a distributed system difficult
    Distribution removes the ability to observe one coherent machine state. Read the lesson →
    When caching is harmful
    Caching is harmful when maintenance and correctness cost exceed saved work. Read the lesson →
    When not to use microservices
    Avoid microservices when the domain is still changing rapidly, the team cannot operate independent services safely, or scale and isolation do not require them. Read the lesson →
    Why caching works
    Caching works when requests reuse data or nearby data often enough to avoid more expensive work. Read the lesson →
    Wide-column stores
    Wide-column systems organize data around partition keys and ordered clustering dimensions in common implementations. Read the lesson →
    Workflow engines
    A workflow engine persists execution progress and resumes work after failures under its programming model. Read the lesson →
    Write-ahead logging
    Write-ahead logging records recovery information before the corresponding dirty data pages are considered safely persisted. Read the lesson →
    Zero-trust principles
    Zero-trust principles reject implicit authorization based solely on network location. Read the lesson →

    No terms match that search.

    THE VISUAL INDEX

    Every diagram has a job

    575 original figures: chapter mechanisms, full-design views, and the required unit plates. The separate master map is Figure M.1.

    FIG. 1.1.1

    The boundary follows the promise

    It separates the user-visible obligation from the process that happens to run the code.

    FIG. 1.1.2

    Data becomes state through a transition

    A concrete transition exposes both the state owner and the effect that a retry could duplicate.

    FIG. 1.1.3

    HLD and LLD ask connected questions

    Both views must agree about who commits state and who reports success.

    FIG. 1.1.4

    From a working demo to a recoverable write

    The improvement is tied to a reproducible failure rather than an arbitrary desire for more components.

    FIG. 1.2.1

    An innocent feature crosses every responsibility

    Dependency arrows identify the concrete knowledge that makes a change spread.

    FIG. 1.2.2

    Separate responsibilities inside one process

    A module boundary can reduce change propagation without adding a network boundary.

    FIG. 1.2.3

    Dependency direction differs from execution direction

    It prevents the common mistake of interpreting every diagram arrow as a network request.

    FIG. 1.2.4

    Abstraction narrows the question at each layer

    Abstraction reduces what a caller must know; it cannot remove physical dependencies.

    FIG. 1.3.1

    Make a vague quality measurable

    A precise scope makes a design falsifiable and reveals the assumptions still needing discussion.

    FIG. 1.3.2

    A decision is a testable hypothesis

    It keeps a previously sensible choice from becoming an unquestioned permanent rule.

    FIG. 1.3.3

    A hard constraint comes before a preference score

    It distinguishes a preference trade-off from violating an invariant.

    FIG. 1.3.4

    Healthy traffic does not prove durable data

    Separate evidence prevents an uptime dashboard from being treated as proof of data safety.

    FIG. 1.4.1

    C4 changes the level of detail

    Choose the view that answers a real reader question, rather than drawing all four levels automatically.

    FIG. 1.4.2

    A deployment view locates the single points of failure

    Deployment placement exposes correlated failure that logical component boxes can hide.

    FIG. 1.4.3

    A lost response makes the outcome uncertain

    A sequence explains the ambiguity that a static architecture diagram leaves out.

    FIG. 1.4.4

    Architecture evolves when an assumption fails

    The sequence is a set of justified changes, not a universal maturity ladder.

    THE FORMULA REFERENCE

    Symbols with assumptions

    Every indexed model is introduced in the lessons. Inputs and guarantee boundaries accompany the notation.

    State transition

    T(S, c) → (S′, result)

    Identify valid state changes and preserved invariants. This abstracts away implementation and failures.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Weighted preference

    score(a) = Σ wᵢ sᵢ(a) / Σ wᵢ

    Use nonnegative weights with positive total. Compare only feasible designs. Scores are illustrative judgments, not benchmark results.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Request rate

    λ = daily users × requests per user per day / 86,400

    An average workload estimate. Peak factors must be assumed or measured separately.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Little’s Law

    L = λ W

    Long-run stable averages with consistent boundaries and units. It is not a universal p99 prediction.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Amdahl’s Law

    speedup(N) = 1 / [(1 − p) + p/N]

    Idealized fixed workload and parallel fraction p; excludes extra coordination overhead unless modeled.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Storage growth

    bytes/day = records/day × bytes/record × retained copies

    Account separately for indexes, compression, retention, metadata, and headroom.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Error allowance

    allowed bad events = (1 − target fraction) × eligible events

    Valid for an event-based SLO; time-based objectives need their own denominator.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Token refill

    tokens′ = min(capacity, tokens + refill_rate × elapsed)

    Admission consumes tokens atomically. Distributed clocks and state ownership need additional design.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Quorum intersection

    R + W > N

    An intersection condition for reads and writes on a fixed replica set. Not by itself a proof of linearizability.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Cost per outcome

    cost / successful business outcomes

    Define accounting period and include capacity, storage, networking, telemetry, and operational work where relevant.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Ideal M/M/1 mean residence

    W = S / (1 − rho)

    Stable single-server Markovian model, rho < 1. A mean model, not a p99 prediction.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Fan-out slow probability

    P(any slow) = 1 − (1 − p)^N

    Requires independent equal-probability call outcomes in this model. Shared failures can correlate tails.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Retry amplification

    maximum attempts = a^L

    a allowed attempts at each of L nested independently retrying layers; actual execution can terminate earlier.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Busy-capacity worksheet

    instances = ceil(peak RPS / (assumed capacity × utilization target))

    Capacity is an explicit hypothetical or tested input; other bottlenecks and surviving failure capacity remain separate.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Error-budget burn

    burn = observed bad fraction / allowed bad fraction

    Use the same eligible-event denominator and a positive allowance.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Cache service-time average

    E[T] = h × T_hit + (1 − h) × T_miss

    A simple service-time mixture, excluding queue effects, dependence, and tail inference.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Backlog growth

    growth/s = arrival/s − completion/s

    Sustained positive growth requires rejection, reduction, or more useful capacity; a bigger queue only changes waiting.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Raw daily storage

    bytes/day = records/s × bytes/record × 86400

    Add indexes, history, metadata, replication, retention, compression and migration separately.

    Derivation and worked example →

    What the evidence means

    Content checks establish presence, exact syllabus allocation, figures, references, and assessment. Executable examples test bounded arithmetic and local invariants. Browser checks test reading, interactions, layouts, offline behavior, and print assembly. The book does not report illustrative objectives as measured production achievements or toy protocols as reviewed production consensus, security, or financial integrations.

    The original request is retained in BRIEF.txt. Additional optional case subjects are suggestions beyond the twelve mandatory worked designs, not omitted required chapters.
